verse.text: Since many have undertaken to compile an account of the things that have been fulfilled among us,
verse.note: The verb can mean to bring something to completion or to convince someone fully. The KJV took it the second way; most modern scholars and versions take it the first way, of events that have run their full course, probably with the overtone that God’s promises were carried out in them.

verse.text: just as they were handed down to us by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word,
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary one for passing teaching or testimony from one generation to the next. Older versions have “delivered”, which no longer conveys that sense; several modern versions already use “handed down” or “handed on”.

verse.text: it seemed good to me also, having followed everything carefully from the start, to write it out for you in order, most excellent Theophilus,
so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught.
verse.note: The verb can mean formal instruction or simply being told a report, as it does in Acts 21:21. On the first reading Theophilus is a believer who has received Christian teaching; on the second he may be an interested outsider who has heard about these events. Most scholars favor instruction, but the question remains open.

verse.text: In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah. His wife was from the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth.
verse.note: The priests were organized into twenty-four divisions, each named for an ancestral head; Abijah’s is the eighth in the list in 1 Chronicles 24. The divisions took turns serving at the temple for a week at a time, so an ordinary priest spent most of the year at home.

verse.text: Both of them were righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and righteous requirements of the Lord.
verse.note: The Greek word belongs to the same family as “righteous” earlier in the verse, a link the usual renderings hide. Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice), so the same root can surface in English under either. The meaning here, the specific things God requires, is not disputed.

verse.text: But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were well advanced in their days.
Now while Zechariah was serving as priest before God, when his division was on duty,
he was chosen by lot, according to the custom of the priesthood, to enter the sanctuary of the Lord and burn incense.
verse.note: Greek has one word for the whole temple complex with its courts and another, used here, for the building itself where God was held to dwell. Only priests entered that building, which is why the people wait outside in verse 10. Most English versions use “temple” for both words, though the NRSV also has “sanctuary” in this passage.

verse.text: The whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of the incense offering.
Then an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar of incense.
Zechariah was troubled when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.
But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you are to name him John.

text.q: You will have joy and delight, and many will rejoice at his birth,
for he will be great before the Lord. He must never drink wine or beer, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb.

verse.note: The Greek word is borrowed from Hebrew and covers intoxicating drinks not made from grapes, most commonly beer brewed from grain. “Strong drink” now suggests distilled spirits, which were unknown in the ancient world. Some versions have “other fermented drink”, and the exact range of the term is uncertain.

text.q: He will turn many of the children of Israel back to the Lord their God.

He himself will go on before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared.”

verse.text: Zechariah said to the angel, “How will I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is well advanced in her days.”
The angel answered him, “I am Gabriel, who stands before God, and I was sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news.

text.q: And look, you will be silent and unable to speak until the day these things happen, because you did not believe my words, which will be fulfilled in their time.”

verse.text: Meanwhile the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they were amazed that he was taking so long in the sanctuary.
When he came out he could not speak to them, and they realized that he had seen a vision in the sanctuary. He kept making signs to them and remained mute.
When his days of service were completed, he went back to his home.
After those days his wife Elizabeth conceived, and she kept herself hidden for five months, saying,

text.q: “This is what the Lord has done for me in the days when he looked on me, to take away my disgrace among people.”

verse.text: In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a town in Galilee named Nazareth,
to a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph, of the house of David. The virgin’s name was Mary.
He came to her and said, “Greetings, favored one! The Lord is with you.”
verse.note: The Greek is a single participle meaning one who has been shown favor, and it is taken up in verse 30, “you have found favor with God”. “Full of grace” comes from the Latin Bible and can suggest a quality Mary possesses, where the Greek describes something done for her. The word for “Greetings” is the ordinary Greek salutation, though some hear in it its literal sense, “rejoice”.

note.traditional: The Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women (KJV)

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add “Blessed are you among women” at the end of the greeting. The earliest witnesses lack the words, and they are generally thought to have been copied in from Elizabeth’s greeting in verse 42.

verse.text: But she was deeply troubled at his words and pondered what kind of greeting this might be.
The angel said to her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God.

text.q: Look, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you are to name him Jesus.
He will be great and will be called Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David.
He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.”

verse.text: Mary said to the angel, “How will this be, since I have never been with a man?”

note.term: since I have never been with a man
note.traditional: seeing I know not a man; since I am a virgin

verse.note: Literally “since I do not know a man”, using the biblical idiom in which “know” refers to sexual relations. The literal form can be misheard today as a statement about acquaintance, so the idiom is translated by its meaning.

verse.text: The angel answered her, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God.

note.term: the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God
note.traditional: that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God (KJV)

verse.note: The Greek can also be read “the holy one to be born will be called Son of God”, taking “holy” with the one born instead of with “called”. Both readings are grammatical and both have scholarly support; the choice does not change the main claim of the verse.

text.q: And look, your relative Elizabeth has also conceived a son in her old age, and this is the sixth month for her who was called barren.
For no word from God will fail.”

note.term: no word from God will fail
note.traditional: nothing will be impossible with God

verse.note: The Greek says literally that “every word from God will not be powerless”, echoing the question put to Abraham about Sarah’s child in Genesis 18:14. The noun can mean “thing” as well as “word”, which gives the traditional rendering; that rendering also fits a slightly different text found in many manuscripts (“with God” for “from God”). “Word” is kept here because Mary takes it up at once in verse 38, “according to your word”.

verse.text: Mary said, “Look, I am the Lord’s slave. May it happen to me according to your word.” Then the angel left her.
verse.note: The Greek is the ordinary feminine word for a slave, someone who belongs to a master, not a hired servant. In the Septuagint it is also how a woman speaks of herself before God or a superior, as Hannah does in 1 Samuel 1:11, so it expresses belonging and readiness more than degradation. Most versions soften it to “servant”; “handmaid” is the older form.

verse.text: In those days Mary set out and went in haste to the hill country, to a town of Judah.
She entered the house of Zechariah and greeted Elizabeth.
When Elizabeth heard Mary’s greeting, the baby leaped in her womb, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit.
She cried out with a loud voice and said, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!

text.q: And why has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
For look, when the sound of your greeting reached my ears, the baby in my womb leaped with delight.
And blessed is she who believed that what was spoken to her from the Lord would be accomplished.”

verse.text: And Mary said, “My soul proclaims the greatness of the Lord,
verse.note: The verb means to make great and, with God as its object, to declare great or extol. “Magnifies” is the traditional rendering, from which the song gets its Latin name, the Magnificat, but in current English the word suggests enlarging an image. The same verb returns in verse 58, where the Lord “had shown the greatness of his mercy”.

text.q: and my spirit delights in God my Savior,
for he has looked on the lowliness of his slave. For look, from now on all generations will call me blessed,
for the Mighty One has done great things for me, and holy is his name.
His mercy is for those who fear him, from generation to generation.
He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered those who are proud in the thoughts of their hearts.
He has brought down rulers from thrones and lifted up the lowly;
the hungry he has filled with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty.
He has come to the aid of Israel his servant, remembering mercy,
just as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and his offspring forever.”

verse.text: Mary stayed with her about three months and then returned to her home.
Now the time came for Elizabeth to give birth, and she bore a son.
Her neighbors and relatives heard that the Lord had shown the greatness of his mercy to her, and they rejoiced with her.
On the eighth day they came to circumcise the child, and they were going to call him Zechariah, after his father.
But his mother spoke up and said, “No! He will be called John.”
They said to her, “There is no one among your relatives who is called by that name.”
Then they made signs to his father to ask what he wanted him to be called.
He asked for a writing tablet and wrote, “John is his name.” And they were all amazed.
At once his mouth was opened and his tongue set free, and he began to speak, blessing God.
Fear came on all who lived around them, and all these things were talked about throughout the hill country of Judea.
All who heard them stored them up in their hearts, saying, “What then will this child be?” For indeed the hand of the Lord was with him.
His father Zechariah was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying,

text.q: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, for he has visited his people and worked redemption for them,
and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David,
just as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old,
salvation from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us,
to show mercy to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant,
the oath that he swore to Abraham our father, to grant us
that we, rescued from the hand of enemies, might serve him without fear
in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.
And you, child, will be called prophet of the Most High, for you will go before the Lord to prepare his ways,
to give his people knowledge of salvation in the forgiveness of their sins,
through the tender mercy of our God, by which the dawn from on high will visit us,

note.traditional: the dayspring from on high; the sunrise

verse.note: The word means a rising, usually of the sun or a star, and the next line about light for those in darkness supports “dawn”. In the Septuagint the same word also translates the Hebrew for the “Branch”, a title of the coming Davidic king (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; 6:12), and many scholars think both images are in view.

Many manuscripts read the past tense, “has visited”, matching verse 68. The future is found in the earliest witnesses and is the reading translated here; the past tense is usually explained as an adjustment to the earlier verse.

text.q: to shine on those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.”

verse.text: The child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the wilderness until the day of his public appearance to Israel.
In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered.
verse.note: The Greek word means “the inhabited world” and in this period was commonly used, with some exaggeration, for the lands under Roman rule. The registration was an enrollment of the population for tax purposes, which is why older versions have “taxed”.

verse.text: (This was the first registration, made when Quirinius was governor of Syria.)

note.traditional: this was the first registration when Quirinius was governor of Syria

verse.note: The dating is a well-known historical difficulty. Josephus places a census under Quirinius in AD 6, about a decade after the death of Herod the Great, in whose reign Luke sets the birth. Some scholars therefore take the Greek to mean “this registration took place before Quirinius was governor of Syria”, which is possible but strained; most take it as translated here and leave the historical question open.

verse.text: And everyone went to be registered, each to his own town.
Joseph also went up from Galilee, from the town of Nazareth, to Judea, to the town of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David,
to be registered with Mary, who was betrothed to him and was pregnant.
While they were there, the days were completed for her to give birth,
and she gave birth to her firstborn son. She wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger, because there was no space for them in the guest room.
verse.note: The traditional “inn” suggests a commercial lodging house, but the Greek word means a place to stay and is the word Luke uses for the “guest room” of the last supper (22:11). For a commercial inn he uses a different word (10:34). Many scholars think the guest quarters of a family home are meant, with the manger in the part of the house where animals were kept, though a public lodging place cannot be ruled out.

verse.text: In that same region there were shepherds living out in the fields and keeping watch over their flock by night.
An angel of the Lord stood before them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were filled with great fear.
And the angel said to them, “Do not be afraid, for look, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people:

text.q: today in the town of David a Savior has been born for you, who is the Messiah, the Lord.

verse.note: The Greek word is a title meaning the anointed king Israel was waiting for, not a surname, and “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader where the title is the point. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels. The Greek here places the two titles side by side without articles, an unusual combination that could also be read as “an anointed Lord”.

text.q: And this will be the sign for you: you will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger.”

verse.text: And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly army, praising God and saying,
verse.note: “Host” is an old English word for an army, and that is what the Greek means: the troops of heaven, a Septuagint expression for the angels or the stars. Most translations keep “host”, which modern readers no longer hear as military. The image of an army announcing peace is part of the scene’s effect.

text.q: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people he favors.”

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read a genitive, literally “among people of good pleasure”, and this is the text translated. Later manuscripts have a nominative, giving the familiar “peace, good will toward men”. The good pleasure is God’s, as comparable Hebrew expressions in the Dead Sea Scrolls show: peace is for those on whom his favor rests, not for people who show goodwill.

verse.text: When the angels had gone away from them into heaven, the shepherds began saying to one another, “Let us go over to Bethlehem, then, and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.”
So they went in haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in the manger.
When they had seen it, they made known what had been told them about this child.
And all who heard were amazed at what the shepherds told them,
but Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart.
And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all that they had heard and seen, just as it had been told them.
When eight days were completed and it was time to circumcise him, he was given the name Jesus, the name the angel had given him before he was conceived in the womb.
And when the days of their purification were completed according to the Law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord,
verse.note: Leviticus 12 prescribes purification only for the mother, forty days after the birth of a son, so the plural “their” is unexpected. It may loosely include Joseph or the child, or may simply mean the purification as the family’s occasion. Some later manuscripts changed it to “her”.

verse.text: as it is written in the Law of the Lord, “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord,”
and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the Law of the Lord: “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”

note.term: “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”

verse.note: Leviticus 12:8 allows this offering for a mother who cannot afford a lamb. A reader who knew the Law would have understood that the family was poor. The presentation of the firstborn (Exodus 13) and the mother’s purification were separate obligations, which Luke narrates together.

verse.text: Now there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon. This man was righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him.
It had been revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord’s Messiah.
Led by the Spirit, he came into the temple. And when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for him what the custom of the Law required,
Simeon himself took him in his arms and blessed God and said,

text.q: “Now you are releasing your slave, Master, in peace, according to your word;

note.traditional: now lettest thou thy servant depart

verse.note: The Greek word means a slave, and “Master” translates the ordinary word for a slave’s owner; the verb is one used for releasing or discharging someone, and also as a gentle expression for dying. Most translations have “servant” and many turn the sentence into a request, but the Greek is a statement: the owner is now letting his slave go. “Servant” remains the mainstream rendering, with “slave” sometimes given in footnotes.

text.q: for my eyes have seen your salvation,
which you have prepared in the sight of all the peoples,
a light for revelation to the Gentiles and for glory to your people Israel.”

verse.note: One Greek word means both “nations” and, in the plural, the non-Jewish peoples; here it stands in contrast to “your people Israel”, so “Gentiles” is used. The grammar also allows “a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and the glory of your people Israel”, with “glory” parallel to “light” and not to “revelation”.

verse.text: And his father and mother were amazed at what was being said about him.
Then Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother, “Look, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel, and to be a sign that is spoken against—

text.q: and a sword will pass through your own soul as well—so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

verse.text: There was also a prophetess, Anna, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She was very advanced in years, having lived with her husband seven years after her marriage,
and then as a widow to the age of eighty-four. She never left the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayers night and day.

note.traditional: a widow of about fourscore and four years

verse.note: The Greek can mean either that Anna was a widow until she reached the age of eighty-four, or that she had been a widow for eighty-four years, which would make her over a hundred. Most translations take the first reading, as here. The phrase rendered “after her marriage” in the previous verse is literally “from her virginity”.

verse.text: Coming up at that very hour, she began giving thanks to God and speaking about the child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
When they had finished everything required by the Law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth.
And the child grew and became strong, being filled with wisdom, and the favor of God was upon him.
Every year his parents went to Jerusalem for the festival of Passover.
When he was twelve years old, they went up as was the custom of the festival,
and when the days were over and they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.
Supposing that he was in the traveling party, they went a day’s journey and then began searching for him among their relatives and acquaintances,
and when they did not find him, they returned to Jerusalem, searching for him.
After three days they found him in the temple, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions.
And all who heard him were astounded at his understanding and his answers.
When his parents saw him, they were astonished, and his mother said to him, “Child, why have you treated us like this? See, your father and I have been looking for you in anguish.”
And he said to them, “Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be in my Father’s house?”
verse.note: The Greek is literally “in the things of my Father”, with no noun. The idiom was regularly used for someone’s house or household, and since the question is where Jesus was to be found, most modern translations and scholars take it that way. The older rendering “about my Father’s business” is also possible.

verse.text: But they did not understand what he said to them.
Then he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and he was subject to them. And his mother kept all these things carefully in her heart.
And Jesus advanced in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and people.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean either bodily height or age and maturity, so the phrase may also be read “in wisdom and in years”. Translations are divided between the two. The verse echoes what is said of the boy Samuel in 1 Samuel 2:26.

verse.text: In the fifteenth year of the rule of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governing Judea, and Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Iturea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene,
verse.note: A tetrarch was the ruler of one part of a divided territory and ranked below a king. This Herod is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great. Counted from the death of Augustus in AD 14, the fifteenth year of Tiberius falls around AD 28–29, though other ways of reckoning the years are possible.

verse.text: during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness.

note.term: during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas

verse.note: The Greek has a singular “high priest” followed by two names, although only one man held the office at a time. Annas was deposed by the Romans around AD 15, and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office from about AD 18 to 36. Luke’s pairing probably reflects the continuing influence of Annas.

verse.text: And he went into all the region around the Jordan, proclaiming a baptism of turning back for the forgiveness of sins,
verse.note: “Repentance” now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word, as used in the Gospels, carries the prophets’ call to return to God, which is a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep “repentance” as an established term understood to include a change of life.

verse.text: as it is written in the book of the words of Isaiah the prophet: “A voice of one crying out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.

text.q: Every valley will be filled, and every mountain and hill will be made low; the crooked will become straight, and the rough ways smooth roads;
and all flesh will see the salvation of God.’”

verse.text: So he said to the crowds that were coming out to be baptized by him, “Brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?

text.q: So produce fruits worthy of that turning back. And do not begin to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones.
Even now the ax is lying at the root of the trees; so every tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.”

verse.text: And the crowds were asking him, “What then should we do?”
He answered them, “Whoever has two tunics must share with the one who has none, and whoever has food must do the same.”
Tax collectors also came to be baptized, and they said to him, “Teacher, what should we do?”
He said to them, “Collect nothing more than what you have been ordered to.”
Soldiers also were asking him, “And we—what should we do?” He said to them, “Do not extort money from anyone by threats or by false accusation, and be content with your pay.”
As the people were waiting expectantly, and all were wondering in their hearts about John, whether he might perhaps be the Messiah,
verse.note: Here the word is a title under discussion, the anointed king Israel was expecting, and not a name. “Messiah” conveys the title to a modern reader, while “Christ” is kept where the word functions as a name for Jesus. Several modern translations make the same distinction.

verse.text: John answered them all: “I baptize you with water, but the one who is stronger than I am is coming; I am not fit to untie the strap of his sandals. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.

note.term: with the Holy Spirit and fire

verse.note: The Greek preposition can mean “with” or “in”, so the phrase may also be read “in the Holy Spirit and fire”. It is disputed whether “fire” stands for purification, for judgment (as in the next verse), or for both. It is also disputed whether one baptism or two is meant.

text.q: His winnowing shovel is in his hand, to clear his threshing floor and gather the wheat into his barn, but the chaff he will burn up with unquenchable fire.”

verse.note: The tool named was a wooden shovel used to throw threshed grain into the wind so that the chaff blew away and the kernels fell. Most modern translations say “winnowing fork”, and older ones “fan”. The standard lexicons give “winnowing shovel”.

verse.text: So, with many other appeals as well, he announced the good news to the people.
verse.note: The Greek verb was an ordinary word for publicly announcing good news. “Gospel” has since become a religious term and a book title. Many modern translations already use “good news” here.

verse.text: But Herod the tetrarch, when he was rebuked by him about Herodias, his brother’s wife, and about all the evil things Herod had done,
verse.note: Herod Antipas had married Herodias, who had been the wife of his half-brother. The Law of Moses forbade marrying a brother’s wife (Leviticus 18:16), which is the basis of John’s rebuke. Luke does not name the brother here.

verse.text: added this to them all as well: he locked John up in prison.
Now when all the people had been baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, heaven was opened,
and the Holy Spirit came down on him in bodily form, like a dove, and a voice came from heaven: “You are my Son, the beloved; with you I am well pleased.”

note.term: “You are my Son, the beloved; with you I am well pleased.”

verse.note: A few witnesses, chiefly Codex Bezae and Old Latin manuscripts, with support in several early Christian writers, read instead “You are my Son; today I have begotten you”, the wording of Psalm 2:7. The great majority of manuscripts have the reading translated here, and most editors accept it. Some scholars argue that the Psalm wording is original.

verse.text: Jesus himself was about thirty years old when he began his work. He was the son, as people supposed, of Joseph, son of Heli,
verse.note: From this point the Greek says only “of Heli, of Matthat” and so on, and “son” is supplied in English. Luke’s list runs backward from Jesus to Adam and differs from Matthew’s in most of the names between Joseph and David. Proposed explanations, such as that one list traces Mary’s line or that one gives legal rather than natural descent, are conjectures.

verse.text: son of Matthat, son of Levi, son of Melchi, son of Jannai, son of Joseph,
son of Mattathias, son of Amos, son of Nahum, son of Esli, son of Naggai,
son of Maath, son of Mattathias, son of Semein, son of Josech, son of Joda,
son of Joanan, son of Rhesa, son of Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, son of Neri,
son of Melchi, son of Addi, son of Cosam, son of Elmadam, son of Er,
son of Joshua, son of Eliezer, son of Jorim, son of Matthat, son of Levi,
son of Simeon, son of Judah, son of Joseph, son of Jonam, son of Eliakim,
son of Melea, son of Menna, son of Mattatha, son of Nathan, son of David,
son of Jesse, son of Obed, son of Boaz, son of Sala, son of Nahshon,
son of Amminadab, son of Admin, son of Arni, son of Hezron, son of Perez, son of Judah,

note.term: son of Admin, son of Arni

verse.note: The manuscripts vary widely here. Many read “son of Aram” or “son of Ram”, matching the Old Testament genealogies, and others have different combinations of names. The form translated is the one printed in the Greek edition followed. In verse 32 that edition’s “Sala” is kept, where other manuscripts have the familiar “Salmon”, and its spelling “Jobel” is given as the familiar “Obed”.

verse.text: son of Jacob, son of Isaac, son of Abraham, son of Terah, son of Nahor,
son of Serug, son of Reu, son of Peleg, son of Eber, son of Shelah,
son of Cainan, son of Arphaxad, son of Shem, son of Noah, son of Lamech,
verse.note: This Cainan, placed between Arphaxad and Shelah, appears in the Greek Septuagint at Genesis 11:12 but not in the Hebrew text, so Luke is following the Greek Bible. The same Greek name in verse 37 is the Kenan of Genesis 5, and is spelled that way there.

verse.text: son of Methuselah, son of Enoch, son of Jared, son of Mahalalel, son of Kenan,
son of Enosh, son of Seth, son of Adam, son of God.
verse.note: The Greek says only “of God”, in the same form as every other link in the list. “Son” is lowercase because the phrase describes Adam’s origin from God and is not the title given to Jesus. Luke probably means the reader to hear it alongside the voice at the baptism and the tempter’s “If you are the Son of God” in the next chapter.

verse.text: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness
for forty days, being tested by the devil. He ate nothing during those days, and when they were over he was hungry.
verse.note: The Greek verb means to put to the test, and in the Greek Old Testament it is the regular word for Israel’s testing in the wilderness, the story from which all three of Jesus’ replies are drawn. Modern “tempt” has narrowed to enticement to sin, which hides that link. Most translations keep “tempted” here, though some recent versions and many commentators prefer “tested”; lexicons recognize both senses.

verse.text: The devil said to him, “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.”
Jesus answered him, “It is written: ‘A person shall not live on bread alone.’”
Then the devil led him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the inhabited world in an instant,
verse.note: Luke does not use the general word for “world” found in Matthew’s parallel but a term for the inhabited earth, which in everyday usage often meant the Roman empire (as in Luke 2:1). Most translations simply have “world.” A first-century reader would have heard a political ring in the offer of these kingdoms.

verse.text: and said to him, “To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been handed over to me, and I give it to whomever I wish.
verse.note: This is the ordinary Greek verb for transferring a person or thing into someone else’s control, and this translation renders it “hand over” wherever it has that sense so the reader can follow the word through the Gospel. The passive leaves unstated who did the handing over. The claim is the devil’s own, and the narrative does not vouch for it.

text.q: So if you worship before me, it will all be yours.”

verse.text: Jesus answered him, “It is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”
Then he brought him to Jerusalem, set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here,
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a projecting tip or edge, and it is not known which part of the temple complex is meant. Suggestions include the southeast corner of the outer wall above the Kidron valley and the roof edge of the sanctuary itself. The traditional “pinnacle” is kept as a neutral term for a high point.

text.q: for it is written: ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’
and: ‘On their hands they will lift you up, so that you do not strike your foot against a stone.’”

verse.text: Jesus answered him, “It has been said: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’”
When the devil had finished every test, he withdrew from him until an opportune time.
verse.note: The noun belongs with the verb rendered “tested” in verse 2 and means a putting to the proof. Most translations have “temptation” here; “test” keeps the connection with the verb and with the wilderness background.

verse.text: Then Jesus returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit, and news about him went out through the whole surrounding region.
He was teaching in their synagogues and was praised by everyone.
He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and as was his custom he went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day. He stood up to read,
and the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him. Unrolling the scroll, he found the place where it was written:

text.q: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to send the oppressed away released,

verse.note: The Greek verb was an ordinary word for announcing good news, used also of public and royal proclamations. “Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a book, so “good news” is used here; many modern translations do the same.

note.traditional: set at liberty those who are oppressed

verse.note: The reading combines Isaiah 61:1–2 with a line from Isaiah 58:6, in the wording of the Greek Old Testament. The noun translated “release” occurs twice; in the Greek Old Testament it is the word for the release of debts and slaves in the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25), and elsewhere in Luke it is the usual word for forgiveness of sins. The rendering keeps both the repeated “release” and the echo between “sent me” and “send.”

text.q: to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.”

verse.text: Then he rolled up the scroll, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on him.
He began by saying to them, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
Everyone spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words coming from his mouth, and they said, “Is this not Joseph’s son?”
verse.note: The Greek says literally that all “were bearing witness to him,” which most interpreters take as approval. A minority reads it as testifying against him, in view of how quickly the mood turns hostile. In the same way, “gracious words” could mean words about God’s grace, and the question about Joseph’s son can be heard as admiring or as dismissive.

verse.text: He said to them, “No doubt you will quote me this proverb: ‘Physician, heal yourself! What we have heard happened in Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.’”
And he said, “Truly I tell you, no prophet finds favor in his hometown.
verse.note: The Greek adjective is the same one used in verse 19 for the year of the Lord’s favor. Most translations have “accepted” or “welcome” here and so lose the echo. The rendering keeps it: the town that hears the year of the Lord’s favor announced shows no favor to the prophet who announces it.

text.q: But I tell you in truth, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the sky was shut for three years and six months and a great famine came over the whole land,

verse.note: The same Greek word covers both the visible sky and God’s dwelling. Here the reference is to the drought in Elijah’s time (1 Kings 17–18), so “sky” is used, as in several modern translations.

text.q: yet Elijah was sent to none of them, only to a widow at Zarephath in the region of Sidon.
And there were many people with skin disease in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, yet none of them was cleansed, only Naaman the Syrian.”

verse.note: The Greek word names those with the condition regulated in Leviticus 13–14, a range of scaly skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean, which is why Naaman is said to be “cleansed.” “Leper” today means someone with Hansen’s disease, which is narrower than the biblical term and may not even be included in it. Most translations keep “lepers,” usually with a footnote saying as much.

verse.text: Everyone in the synagogue was filled with rage on hearing this.
They got up, drove him out of the town, and led him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, intending to throw him off the cliff.
But he passed through the middle of them and went on his way.
He went down to Capernaum, a town in Galilee, and was teaching them on the Sabbath.
They were astounded at his teaching, because his word carried authority.
In the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out in a loud voice,

text.q: “Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God!”

verse.note: The Greek is either an exclamation of surprise or displeasure, or the imperative of a verb meaning “let, leave alone.” Translations are divided between “Ha!” or “Ah!” and “Let us alone!” Either fits the scene.

verse.text: Jesus rebuked him, saying, “Be silent, and come out of him!” The demon threw the man down in their midst and came out of him without doing him any harm.
Amazement came over them all, and they said to one another, “What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!”
And talk about him spread to every place in the surrounding region.
He left the synagogue and went into Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was suffering from a high fever, and they asked him to help her.
Standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and it left her. At once she got up and began to serve them.
As the sun was setting, all who had people sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on each one of them and healed them.
Demons also came out of many, shouting, “You are the Son of God!” But he rebuked them and would not let them speak, because they knew that he was the Messiah.
verse.note: Here the Greek word is a title, the anointed king Israel expected, and not yet a name for Jesus. “Messiah” conveys the title as a first-century Jewish hearer would have heard it. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep “Christ” where the word works as a name.

verse.text: When day came, he went out and made his way to a deserted place. The crowds were looking for him, and when they reached him they tried to keep him from leaving them.
But he said to them, “I must bring the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well, because that is what I was sent for.”
And he went on proclaiming in the synagogues of Judea.
verse.note: Many manuscripts read “Galilee,” which matches Mark 1:39 and the surrounding narrative. The earliest witnesses have “Judea,” and most editors judge that scribes changed it to “Galilee” to remove the difficulty. Luke sometimes uses “Judea” for the whole land of the Jews, Galilee included, and that may be the sense here.

verse.text: Once, while the crowd was pressing in on him and listening to the word of God, he was standing beside Lake Gennesaret,
verse.note: This is the body of water that Matthew and Mark call the Sea of Galilee. Luke consistently uses the ordinary Greek word for a lake, which is the more exact term for an inland body of fresh water. Gennesaret is the name of the fertile plain on its northwestern shore.

verse.text: and he saw two boats lying at the edge of the lake; the fishermen had gotten out of them and were washing their nets.
He got into one of the boats, which was Simon’s, and asked him to put out a little from the land. Then he sat down and taught the crowds from the boat.
When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep water and let down your nets for a catch.”
Simon answered, “Master, we worked hard all through the night and caught nothing. But at your word I will let down the nets.”
verse.note: This form of address occurs only in Luke in the New Testament and is always spoken to Jesus. In ordinary Greek it named someone in charge, such as a supervisor or overseer. Luke uses it where the other Gospels often have “Teacher” or “Rabbi.” It is a different word from “Lord” in verse 8.

verse.text: When they had done this, they enclosed a great number of fish, and their nets were beginning to tear.
So they signaled to their associates in the other boat to come and help them. They came and filled both boats, so that they began to sink.
When Simon Peter saw it, he fell at the knees of Jesus and said, “Go away from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man!”
For amazement had seized him and all who were with him at the catch of fish they had taken,
and likewise James and John, the sons of Zebedee, who were partners with Simon. Then Jesus said to Simon, “Do not be afraid. From now on you will be catching people alive.”
verse.note: Most translations have “catching men” or “fishing for people,” echoing the “fishers” saying in Matthew and Mark. Luke’s verb is not a fishing term; it means to capture alive, and in the Septuagint it is used of sparing captives in war. The rendering keeps that sense: fish are caught to die, but these people are to be taken alive. Its only other New Testament use is 2 Timothy 2:26.

verse.text: And when they had brought the boats to land, they left everything and followed him.
While he was in one of the towns, there was a man covered with leprosy. When he saw Jesus, he fell on his face and begged him, “Lord, if you are willing, you can make me clean.”
verse.note: The Greek word, as in the Greek version of Leviticus 13–14, covers a range of skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean and excluded them from ordinary community life. It is not limited to, and may not include, what is now called leprosy (Hansen’s disease). This is why the man asks to be made “clean” and not simply healed.

verse.text: Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I am willing. Be made clean.” And immediately the leprosy left him.
And he ordered him to tell no one: “Instead, go and show yourself to the priest, and make an offering for your cleansing as Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.”
verse.note: Leviticus 14 requires a person recovered from such a skin disease to be examined by a priest and to bring offerings before returning to normal life. “Them” may be the priests or the people in general, who would then have official evidence of the cure. The Greek could also mean “as a testimony against them,” though most interpreters take it in the neutral sense.

verse.text: But the news about him spread all the more, and large crowds were gathering to hear him and to be healed of their illnesses.
But he would withdraw to deserted places and pray.

One day, while he was teaching, there were Pharisees and teachers of the Law sitting there, who had come from every village of Galilee and Judea and from Jerusalem. And the power of the Lord was with him to heal.

note.term: the power of the Lord was with him to heal
note.traditional: the power of the Lord was present to heal them

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read “him,” making Jesus the one who heals. Many later manuscripts read “them,” giving “the power of the Lord was present to heal them,” the reading behind the King James Version. “The Lord” here refers to God, whose power is at work in Jesus.

verse.text: Just then some men came carrying a paralyzed man on a bed, and they were trying to bring him in and lay him before Jesus.
Finding no way to bring him in because of the crowd, they went up on the roof and let him down through the tiles, stretcher and all, into the middle in front of Jesus.
When he saw their faith, he said, “Man, your sins are forgiven you.”
The scribes and the Pharisees began to reason, saying, “Who is this man who speaks blasphemies? Who can forgive sins except God alone?”
But Jesus, perceiving their reasoning, answered them, “Why are you reasoning in your hearts?

text.q: Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’?

verse.text: But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins—” he said to the paralyzed man, “I tell you, get up, pick up your stretcher, and go to your house.”
At once he stood up in front of them, picked up what he had been lying on, and went off to his house, glorifying God.
Astonishment seized them all, and they glorified God; they were filled with fear and said, “We have seen extraordinary things today.”
After this he went out and saw a tax collector named Levi sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.”
verse.note: These were local collectors of tolls and customs duties on goods, working for contractors who had bought the right to collect. They were widely regarded as dishonest and as collaborators with the ruling powers, which is why they are paired with “sinners” in verse 30. The “tax booth” was a toll station.

verse.text: And leaving everything behind, he got up and followed him.
Then Levi gave a great banquet for him in his house, and there was a large crowd of tax collectors and others who were reclining at table with them.
The Pharisees and their scribes were grumbling to his disciples, saying, “Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?”
Jesus answered them, “Those who are healthy have no need of a doctor, but those who are sick do.

text.q: I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to turning back.”

verse.note: The traditional rendering is “repentance,” and most translations keep it as an established term. In modern English that word centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word here carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, so it is rendered “turning back.”

verse.text: They said to him, “John’s disciples fast often and offer prayers, and so do the disciples of the Pharisees, but yours eat and drink.”
Jesus said to them, “You cannot make the wedding guests fast while the bridegroom is with them, can you?
verse.note: The Greek is literally “sons of the bridal chamber,” a Semitic turn of phrase for those who belong to the wedding party, whether the groom’s attendants or the guests more broadly. A wedding was a time of feasting, at which fasting would be out of place.

text.q: But days will come, and when the bridegroom is taken away from them, then they will fast in those days.”

verse.text: He also told them a parable: “No one tears a patch from a new garment and puts it on an old garment. If he does, he will tear the new garment, and the patch from the new will not match the old.

text.q: And no one puts new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the new wine will burst the skins; it will be spilled, and the skins will be ruined.

verse.note: Wine was stored in sewn animal skins. Newly pressed wine continues to ferment and give off gas; a new skin stretches with it, but an old skin that has already stretched and hardened splits. Greek uses two near-synonyms for “new” in these verses, one for the wine and another for the garment and the skins; both are rendered “new” here.

text.q: But new wine must be put into new wineskins.
And no one who has drunk old wine wants new, for he says, ‘The old is good.’”

verse.note: Many manuscripts read “better” where the earliest have “good”; the comparative looks like a scribal sharpening. A few witnesses, including Codex Bezae, omit the whole verse, which has no parallel in Matthew or Mark. The word for “good” here can also mean pleasant or mellow.

verse.text: One Sabbath he was passing through grainfields, and his disciples were plucking heads of grain, rubbing them in their hands, and eating them.

note.traditional: on the second sabbath after the first

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add a rare word here, literally “second-first,” which the King James Version renders “the second sabbath after the first.” Its meaning is unknown, and the earliest witnesses lack it. Most modern editions and translations omit it, as the text followed here does.

Picking grain by hand in someone else’s field was allowed by the Law (Deuteronomy 23:25), so the charge is not theft. The objection is that plucking and rubbing out the kernels counted as reaping and threshing, which were work forbidden on the Sabbath in the Pharisees’ interpretation.

verse.text: But some of the Pharisees said, “Why are you doing what is not permitted on the Sabbath?”
verse.note: The Greek verb means simply “it is allowed” and does not contain the word for law. Most translations say “lawful,” which is accurate in that the standard in view is the Law of Moses as interpreted, but in modern English it can suggest civil legality. “Permitted” is used throughout this chapter (verses 2, 4 and 9).

verse.text: Jesus answered them, “Have you not even read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him—

text.q: how he entered the house of God, took the bread of the Presence and ate it, and gave some to those with him, though no one is permitted to eat it except the priests alone?”

verse.note: These were twelve loaves set out before God in the sanctuary each Sabbath, which only the priests were to eat when they were replaced (Leviticus 24:5–9). The story of David is told in 1 Samuel 21:1–6. The Greek phrase is literally “the loaves of the setting-out”; “bread of the Presence” is the established English name for them.

verse.text: And he said to them, “The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.”
On another Sabbath he entered the synagogue and was teaching. A man was there whose right hand was withered.
The scribes and the Pharisees were watching him closely to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might find a charge to bring against him.
But he knew their thoughts, and he said to the man with the withered hand, “Get up and stand in the middle.” And he got up and stood there.
Then Jesus said to them, “I ask you: is it permitted on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save a life or to destroy it?”
And looking around at them all, he said to him, “Stretch out your hand.” He did so, and his hand was restored.
But they were filled with senseless fury and began discussing with one another what they might do to Jesus.
verse.note: The Greek word means want of sense or understanding, and can describe either folly or a frenzy that has lost its reason. Older versions have “madness,” and most modern ones have “fury” or “rage.” “Senseless fury” tries to keep both the anger the context implies and the irrationality the word names.

verse.text: In those days he went out to the mountain to pray, and he spent the whole night in prayer to God.
When day came, he called his disciples to him and chose twelve of them, whom he also named apostles:
Simon, whom he also named Peter, and Andrew his brother, and James and John, and Philip and Bartholomew,
and Matthew and Thomas, and James son of Alphaeus, and Simon who was called the Zealot,
verse.note: The word means “zealous one” and corresponds to the Aramaic-based term that Matthew and Mark use for the same Simon. It may mark him as fervent for the Law, or as sympathetic to armed resistance against Rome. Whether an organized party called the Zealots existed this early is disputed, so the label should not be pressed.

verse.text: and Judas son of James, and Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.
verse.note: The Greek says only “Judas of James.” This construction normally names a father, and most modern translations render it “son of James.” The King James Version took it as “brother of James,” identifying him with the Jude of the letter; that is possible but less likely.

verse.text: He came down with them and stood on a level place, with a large crowd of his disciples and a great multitude of the people from all Judea and Jerusalem and the coastal region of Tyre and Sidon,
who had come to hear him and to be cured of their diseases. Those troubled by unclean spirits were being healed,
and the whole crowd was trying to touch him, because power was going out from him and curing them all.
Then he lifted his eyes to his disciples and said: “Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God.

text.q: Blessed are you who are hungry now, for you will be satisfied. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.
Blessed are you when people hate you, and when they shut you out and insult you and reject your name as evil because of the Son of Man.
Rejoice on that day and leap for joy, for look, your reward is great in heaven; for their ancestors treated the prophets the same way.
But woe to you who are rich, for you have been paid your comfort in full.

note.term: you have been paid your comfort in full

verse.note: The verb is the standard term on receipts of the period for acknowledging payment in full, and hearers would have caught the commercial tone. Many modern translations render it “you have received your comfort” or “received in full.” The point is that the rich have nothing further owed to them.

text.q: Woe to you who are full now, for you will go hungry. Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep.
Woe to you when all people speak well of you, for their ancestors treated the false prophets the same way.
But to you who are listening I say: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you,
bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you.
To the one who strikes you on the cheek, offer the other as well, and from the one who takes your cloak, do not withhold your tunic either.
Give to everyone who asks you, and from the one who takes what is yours, do not demand it back.
And as you want people to do to you, do the same to them.
If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them.

note.term: what credit is that to you

verse.note: The word is the one usually translated “grace” or “favor.” Here it may mean thanks or credit earned, or favor in God’s eyes; Matthew’s parallel has “reward.” The same root returns in verse 35, where God is kind to the “ungrateful,” an echo English cannot easily keep.

text.q: And if you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? Even sinners do the same.
And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners, to get back the same amount.
But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing back. Then your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High, because he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil.

verse.note: Elsewhere in Greek of the period this verb means “to despair,” which would give “despairing of nothing,” or, with a variant found in some manuscripts, “despairing of no one.” Most translators and commentators judge that the context, with its contrast to lending in hope of receiving (verse 34), requires “expecting nothing in return,” though that sense is not clearly attested elsewhere this early.

text.q: Be compassionate, just as your Father is compassionate.

verse.note: Nearly all English versions have “merciful” here. The Greek word, however, is not the usual one for mercy but a term for feeling pity or compassion, used in the Septuagint of God as “compassionate and merciful” alongside the ordinary mercy word. “Compassionate” keeps the two distinct; the difference in meaning is slight.

text.q: Do not judge, and you will not be judged. Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Pardon, and you will be pardoned.

note.term: Pardon, and you will be pardoned
note.traditional: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven

verse.note: Most translations have “forgive,” but this is not the usual New Testament verb for forgiving. It means to release or let go, and is used of freeing a prisoner or discharging a debtor. Following “judge” and “condemn,” it continues the courtroom picture, which “pardon” preserves; the practical sense is close to forgiveness.

text.q: Give, and it will be given to you: a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be poured into your lap. For with the measure you use, it will be measured back to you.”

verse.note: The picture is of a grain seller filling a measure generously: packing it down, shaking it to settle, and heaping it until it spills. The buyer received the grain in the fold of the outer garment pulled up over the belt to form a pouch, which is what the Greek word here refers to. The Greek says literally “they will give,” an indefinite plural widely taken to mean that God is the giver.

verse.text: He also told them a parable: “Can a blind person guide a blind person? Will they not both fall into a pit?

text.q: A disciple is not above the teacher, but everyone who is fully trained will be like his teacher.
Why do you look at the speck in your brother’s eye but fail to notice the beam in your own eye?

How can you say to your brother, ‘Brother, let me take out the speck that is in your eye,’ when you yourself do not see the beam in your own eye? Hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take out the speck that is in your brother’s eye.
For no good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit.
For each tree is known by its own fruit. People do not gather figs from thornbushes, nor do they pick grapes from a bramble.
The good person brings out what is good from the good treasure of his heart, and the evil person brings out what is evil from the evil; for his mouth speaks from what overflows the heart.
Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?
Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them—I will show you what that person is like.

He is like a person building a house, who dug down deep and laid a foundation on the rock. When a flood came, the river burst against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built.

But the one who has heard and not done is like a person who built a house on the ground without a foundation. The river burst against it, and at once it collapsed, and the ruin of that house was great.”

verse.text: After he had finished all his sayings in the hearing of the people, he entered Capernaum.
Now a centurion had a slave who was highly valued by him, and this slave was sick and about to die.
verse.note: Older versions have “servant.” The Greek word names a person owned by another, and a first-century reader would have understood “slave”; several modern versions agree. In verse 7 the centurion uses a different word, which can mean “boy,” “child,” or “servant,” and is rendered “servant” there.

verse.text: When he heard about Jesus, he sent elders of the Jews to him, asking him to come and save his slave.
When they came to Jesus, they pleaded with him earnestly, saying, “He is worthy to have you grant him this,

text.q: for he loves our nation, and he himself built the synagogue for us.”

verse.note: This is the same Greek word that in the plural is usually rendered “Gentiles.” In the singular it means a people or nation, and here the Jewish elders use it of their own people.

verse.text: So Jesus went with them. He was already not far from the house when the centurion sent friends to say to him, “Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not fit to have you come under my roof.

text.q: That is why I did not consider myself worthy even to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed.
For I too am a man placed under authority, with soldiers under me. I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my slave, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

verse.text: When Jesus heard this, he was amazed at him. Turning to the crowd that was following him, he said, “I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.”
And when those who had been sent returned to the house, they found the slave in good health.
Soon afterward he went to a town called Nain, and his disciples and a large crowd went with him.
As he came near the gate of the town, a man who had died was being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. A sizable crowd from the town was with her.
When the Lord saw her, he was moved with compassion for her and said to her, “Do not weep.”
Then he came up and touched the bier, and the bearers stood still. He said, “Young man, I say to you, rise!”
The dead man sat up and began to speak, and Jesus gave him to his mother.
verse.note: The wording matches the Greek version of 1 Kings 17:23, where Elijah restores a widow’s dead son and gives him to his mother. Readers who knew that story would hear the echo, which helps explain the crowd’s response in the next verse: “A great prophet has risen among us!”

verse.text: Fear seized them all, and they glorified God, saying, “A great prophet has risen among us!” and “God has visited his people!”
This report about him spread through the whole of Judea and all the surrounding region.
John’s disciples reported all these things to him. Calling two of his disciples to him, John
sent them to the Lord to ask, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?”
When the men came to him, they said, “John the Baptist has sent us to you to ask, ‘Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?’”
In that hour he healed many people of diseases, afflictions, and evil spirits, and to many who were blind he granted sight.

Then he answered them, “Go and report to John what you have seen and heard: the blind see again, the lame walk, those with skin disease are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, the poor have good news announced to them.
verse.note: Most versions keep “lepers.” The Greek term names people with the range of scaly skin conditions regulated in Leviticus 13–14, which made a person ritually unclean; that is why they are “cleansed” and not simply healed. Modern “leprosy” (Hansen’s disease) is narrower and may not even be included. Scholars widely agree on this, though many translations keep the familiar word and explain it in a footnote.

note.term: have good news announced to them
note.traditional: have the gospel preached to them

verse.note: The Greek verb was an ordinary word for announcing good news, while “gospel” is now a religious term or a book title; many modern versions also have “good news” here. The whole list echoes Isaiah’s pictures of the time of God’s salvation (Isaiah 35:5–6; 61:1), which is the point of the answer sent to John.

text.q: And blessed is anyone who does not stumble because of me.”

verse.note: The verb comes from a word for a trap or obstacle and means being tripped up in one’s trust or loyalty. “Offended” now suggests hurt feelings, which is too weak. Modern versions divide here between “takes no offense at me” and “does not stumble on account of me.”

verse.text: When John’s messengers had left, he began to speak to the crowds about John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to look at? A reed shaken by the wind?

text.q: What, then, did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Look, those who wear splendid clothing and live in luxury are in royal palaces.
What, then, did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Look, I am sending my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way ahead of you.’
I tell you, among those born of women no one is greater than John; yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.”

verse.text: (And all the people who heard, even the tax collectors, vindicated God, having been baptized with John’s baptism.
verse.note: The verb belongs to a single Greek word family that English splits in two (“righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice,” “justify”). Here it means to declare someone to be in the right: by accepting John’s baptism the people affirmed that God’s call through John was right. Many modern versions paraphrase as “acknowledged God’s justice” or “declared God just.” The same verb returns in verse 35.

Verses 29–30 are taken here, with the punctuation of the Greek edition translated, as the narrator’s aside. They can also be read as a continuation of Jesus’s own words about John. It is likewise unclear whether what the people “heard” was John’s preaching or what Jesus has just said.

verse.text: But the Pharisees and the experts in the law rejected God’s purpose for themselves, not having been baptized by him.)
verse.note: The word names men learned in the Law of Moses and its interpretation, a group overlapping with the scribes. “Lawyer” now suggests an attorney representing clients in court. Several modern versions use “experts in the law”; others keep “lawyers.”

text.q: “To what, then, shall I compare the people of this generation, and what are they like?
They are like children sitting in the marketplace and calling out to one another, saying, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep.’
For John the Baptist has come eating no bread and drinking no wine, and you say, ‘He has a demon.’
The Son of Man has come eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’
Yet wisdom is vindicated by all her children.”

verse.text: One of the Pharisees asked him to eat with him, and he went into the Pharisee’s house and reclined at the table.
And there was a woman in the town who was a sinner. When she learned that he was reclining at the table in the Pharisee’s house, she brought an alabaster jar of perfume
and stood behind him at his feet, weeping. With her tears she began to wet his feet, and she kept wiping them with the hair of her head, kissing his feet and anointing them with the perfume.

note.term: stood behind him at his feet

verse.note: At a formal meal guests reclined on low couches, leaning on the left elbow with their feet stretched out away from the table. This is how the woman could stand behind Jesus and still reach his feet.

verse.text: When the Pharisee who had invited him saw this, he said to himself, “If this man were a prophet, he would know who and what kind of woman this is who is touching him—that she is a sinner.”
Jesus answered him, “Simon, I have something to say to you.” And he said, “Teacher, say it.”

text.q: “A certain moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty.

verse.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s wage for a laborer. The two debts are therefore well over a year’s wages and about two months’ wages.

text.q: Since they had nothing to repay him with, he canceled the debts of both. Which of them, then, will love him more?”

verse.text: Simon answered, “I suppose the one for whom he canceled the larger debt.” And he said to him, “You have judged rightly.”
Then, turning to the woman, he said to Simon, “Do you see this woman? I came into your house; you gave me no water for my feet, but she has wet my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.

text.q: You gave me no kiss, but she, from the time I came in, has not stopped kissing my feet.
You did not anoint my head with oil, but she has anointed my feet with perfume.
For this reason, I tell you, her sins, many as they are, have been forgiven, for she loved much. But the one who is forgiven little loves little.”

verse.note: The Greek conjunction can give either the cause of something or the evidence for it. The parable, in which love follows the canceling of a debt, and the second half of the verse favor the second sense: her great love shows that she has been forgiven. Most interpreters read it this way, though an older reading takes her love as the reason for her forgiveness.

verse.text: Then he said to her, “Your sins have been forgiven.”
Those reclining at the table with him began to say among themselves, “Who is this, who even forgives sins?”
But he said to the woman, “Your faith has saved you; go in peace.”
Soon afterward he was traveling from town to town and village to village, proclaiming and announcing the good news of the kingdom of God. The Twelve were with him,
as were some women who had been cured of evil spirits and illnesses: Mary, the one called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out;
Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward; Susanna; and many others, who were providing for them out of their own resources.
verse.note: Herod here is Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. The Greek word covers the manager of a household or estate; Chuza’s exact post is unknown, but it implies that Joanna was a woman of means and standing. Luke notes that women like her paid for the travels of Jesus and the Twelve out of their own property.

verse.text: As a large crowd was gathering and people from town after town were making their way to him, he spoke by way of a parable:

text.q: “A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was trampled, and the birds of the sky ate it up.
Other seed fell on the rock, and when it grew up it withered, because it had no moisture.
Other seed fell among the thorns, and the thorns grew up with it and choked it.

verse.text: And other seed fell into the good soil, and when it grew up it yielded fruit a hundred times over.” As he said these things, he called out, “Whoever has ears to hear, let them hear!”
His disciples asked him what this parable meant.
He said, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of God, but for the rest it comes in parables, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “mysteries,” which most English versions keep as an established technical term. In Jewish Greek of the period the word ordinarily meant a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose, whereas English “mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding. Several modern versions also use “secrets” in this saying.

The words that follow echo Isaiah 6:9–10. The Greek conjunction normally expresses purpose, and it is rendered that way here. Some interpreters take it as expressing result (“with the result that”) or as shorthand for “so that the Scripture might be fulfilled.” The question has long been debated.

text.q: Now this is what the parable means: the seed is the word of God.
Those along the path are the ones who have heard; then the devil comes and takes away the word from their hearts, so that they may not believe and be saved.
Those on the rock are the ones who, when they hear, receive the word with joy. But these have no root; they believe for a time, and in a time of testing they fall away.

verse.note: The King James tradition has “temptation.” In this period the word mainly meant a putting to the proof, an ordeal that shows whether someone will stay faithful, while English “temptation” has narrowed to enticement to sin. Most modern versions likewise have “testing” or “trial” in this verse.

text.q: As for what fell among the thorns, these are the ones who have heard, but as they go on their way they are choked by the worries and wealth and pleasures of life, and they bring no fruit to maturity.
But as for what is in the fine soil, these are the ones who, having heard the word with a fine and good heart, hold on to it and bear fruit with endurance.

verse.note: The pairing of these two adjectives was a stock Greek expression for a person of excellent character. Luke’s Greek-speaking readers would have recognized it. The word translated “fine” is the same one used of the soil earlier in the verse.

text.q: No one lights a lamp and covers it with a jar or puts it under a bed. Instead, they put it on a lampstand, so that those who come in may see the light.
For nothing is hidden that will not come to light, and nothing concealed that will not be known and come to light.
So take care how you hear. For to the one who has, it will be given; and from the one who does not have, even what they think they have will be taken away.”

verse.text: His mother and brothers came to where he was, but they could not get to him because of the crowd.
It was reported to him, “Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, wanting to see you.”
But he answered them, “My mother and my brothers are these: those who hear the word of God and do it.”
One day he got into a boat with his disciples, and he said to them, “Let us cross over to the other side of the lake.” So they set sail.
As they sailed, he fell asleep. A windstorm came down on the lake, and they were being swamped and were in danger.
They went to him and woke him, saying, “Master, Master, we are perishing!” He woke up and rebuked the wind and the surging water, and they stopped, and there was a calm.
He said to them, “Where is your faith?” In fear and amazement they said to one another, “Who then is this, that he gives orders even to the winds and the water, and they obey him?”
They sailed down to the region of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee.
verse.note: Manuscripts vary here and in verse 37 among “Gerasenes,” “Gadarenes,” and “Gergesenes,” as they do in the parallel accounts in Matthew and Mark. The city of Gerasa lay well inland from the lake, which probably prompted the alternative readings. SBLGNT reads “Gerasenes.”

verse.text: As he stepped out onto the land, a man from the town who had demons met him. For a long time he had worn no clothes, and he did not live in a house but among the tombs.
When he saw Jesus, he cried out and fell down before him and said in a loud voice, “What do you want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg you, do not torment me!”

For Jesus had been commanding the unclean spirit to come out of the man. Many times it had seized him; he would be bound with chains and shackles and kept under guard, and breaking the bonds he would be driven by the demon into the deserted places.
verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean “on many occasions” or “for a long time.” The first is chosen here because the sentence goes on to describe repeated episodes of binding and escape. A number of translators prefer the second.

verse.text: Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He said, “Legion,” because many demons had entered him.
verse.note: The word is borrowed from Latin. A legion was the main unit of the Roman army, roughly five thousand soldiers at full strength, so the name signals a vast and organized force. To people living under Roman rule it may also have carried overtones of military occupation, though this is debated.

verse.text: And they kept pleading with him not to order them to go off into the abyss.
verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament this word names the primeval deep. In Jewish writings of the period it had also come to mean the underworld prison where rebellious spirits are confined, and that is what the demons fear here. Revelation 9 and 20 use the word in the same way.

verse.text: Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and the demons pleaded with him to permit them to enter those pigs; and he permitted them.
The demons came out of the man and entered the pigs, and the herd rushed down the steep bank into the lake and drowned.
When the herdsmen saw what had happened, they fled and reported it in the town and in the countryside.
People came out to see what had happened. They came to Jesus and found the man from whom the demons had gone out sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid.
Those who had seen it reported to them how the man possessed by demons had been saved.
verse.note: Most versions have “healed” here and “made you well” or “made well” in verses 48 and 50. The Greek verb means to rescue or deliver, whether from illness, danger, or death, and Luke uses the same word in verse 12 of final salvation. “Saved” is kept throughout the chapter so the repetition can be heard; verse 48 repeats word for word what Jesus said to the forgiven woman at 7:50.

verse.text: Then the whole population of the surrounding region of the Gerasenes asked him to leave them, because they were gripped by great fear. So he got into a boat to return.
The man from whom the demons had gone out begged to be with him, but Jesus sent him away, saying,
“Return to your home, and recount all that God has done for you.” And he went away, proclaiming throughout the whole town all that Jesus had done for him.
When Jesus returned, the crowd welcomed him, for they were all expecting him.
Just then a man named Jairus came, who was a leader of the synagogue. He fell at the feet of Jesus and pleaded with him to come to his house,
because he had an only daughter, about twelve years old, and she was dying. As Jesus went, the crowds were crushing him.
