And there was a woman who had had a flow of blood for twelve years; though she had spent her whole livelihood on physicians, she could not be cured by anyone.

note.term: though she had spent her whole livelihood on physicians

verse.note: This clause is absent from some important early manuscripts, and some scholars think it was added by copyists from the parallel in Mark 5:26. Some critical editions enclose it in brackets as doubtful. SBLGNT prints it without brackets.

verse.text: She came up behind him and touched the fringe of his cloak, and immediately her flow of blood stopped.
verse.note: The word can mean simply the edge of a garment. In the Greek Old Testament it is also the term for the tassels that the Law required Israelite men to wear on the corners of their cloaks (Numbers 15:38–39). Many interpreters think one of these tassels is meant here.

verse.text: Jesus said, “Who touched me?” When everyone denied it, Peter said, “Master, the crowds are hemming you in and pressing against you.”
But Jesus said, “Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me.”

When the woman saw that she had not gone unnoticed, she came trembling and fell down before him, and in the presence of all the people she reported why she had touched him and how she had been healed immediately.
He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has saved you. Go in peace.”
While he was still speaking, someone came from the synagogue leader’s house and said, “Your daughter has died. Do not trouble the teacher any longer.”
But Jesus heard this and answered him, “Do not be afraid. Only believe, and she will be saved.”
When he came to the house, he did not let anyone go in with him except Peter and John and James and the child’s father and mother.
Everyone was weeping and mourning for her. But he said, “Do not weep, for she has not died but is sleeping.”
And they laughed at him, knowing that she had died.
But he took hold of her hand and called out, “Child, get up!”
Her spirit came back, and she stood up immediately, and he directed that she be given something to eat.
Her parents were astounded, but he commanded them to tell no one what had happened.
Jesus called the Twelve together and gave them power and authority over all the demons and to cure diseases,
and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal the sick.
He said to them, “Take nothing for the road—no staff, no bag, no bread, no money—and do not have two tunics each.

text.q: Whatever house you enter, stay there, and leave from there.
And wherever people do not welcome you, as you leave that town shake the dust off your feet as a testimony against them.”

verse.text: So they set out and went from village to village, proclaiming the good news and curing people everywhere.
verse.note: The Greek verb was an ordinary word for announcing good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. “Gospel” now sounds like a religious term or a book title, so the plain sense is given here. Many modern translations alternate between “good news” and “gospel”.

verse.text: Now Herod the tetrarch heard about everything that was happening, and he was greatly perplexed, because it was being said by some that John had been raised from the dead,
by some that Elijah had appeared, and by others that one of the ancient prophets had risen.
But Herod said, “John I beheaded. So who is this about whom I hear such things?” And he kept trying to see him.
When the apostles returned, they recounted to Jesus all they had done. Taking them along, he withdrew privately to a town called Bethsaida.
But the crowds found out and followed him. He welcomed them and spoke to them about the kingdom of God, and healed those who needed a cure.

Now the day began to decline, and the Twelve came and said to him, “Send the crowd away, so that they can go to the surrounding villages and farms to find lodging and get provisions, because we are in a deserted place here.”
But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.” They said, “We have no more than five loaves and two fish—unless we ourselves are to go and buy food for all these people.”
For there were about five thousand men. He said to his disciples, “Have them recline in groups of about fifty each.”
verse.note: The verb means to recline for a meal, the normal posture at a formal dinner or banquet in the period. Most English versions say “sit down”, which is natural English but loses the suggestion that the crowd is being arranged as guests for a meal.

verse.text: They did so and had everyone recline.
Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, blessed them, broke them, and kept giving them to the disciples to set before the crowd.
They all ate and were filled, and what they had left over was picked up: twelve baskets of broken pieces.
Once, when he was praying in private and the disciples were with him, he asked them, “Who do the crowds say I am?”
They answered, “John the Baptist; but others, Elijah; and others, that one of the ancient prophets has risen.”
He said to them, “But you—who do you say I am?” Peter answered, “The Messiah of God.”
verse.note: Peter is identifying Jesus with a title, the anointed king Israel was waiting for, not using a name. “Messiah” conveys that title to a modern reader, where “Christ” tends to be heard as a surname. Several modern translations use “Messiah” in the Gospels for the same reason.

verse.text: But he sternly warned them and ordered them to tell this to no one,
saying, “The Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.”
Then he said to them all, “If anyone wants to come after me, let them deny themselves, take up their cross daily, and follow me.

text.q: For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for my sake—that one will save it.
For what good does it do a person to gain the whole world and yet lose or forfeit their own self?
For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, the Son of Man will be ashamed of that person when he comes in his glory and that of the Father and of the holy angels.
But I tell you truly, there are some standing here who will certainly not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.”

verse.text: About eight days after these words, he took along Peter, John, and James and went up the mountain to pray.
And as he was praying, the appearance of his face became different, and his clothing became white, flashing like lightning.
And look, two men were talking with him—they were Moses and Elijah,
who appeared in glory and were speaking of his departure, which he was about to fulfill in Jerusalem.
verse.note: The Greek word is exodos. It was an ordinary word for a going out and a recognized euphemism for death, but it was also the name of Israel’s deliverance from Egypt. With Moses standing there, many scholars think Luke intends the echo: Jesus’ death, resurrection and ascension in Jerusalem as a new act of deliverance.

verse.text: Now Peter and those with him were weighed down with sleep; but when they became fully awake, they saw his glory and the two men standing with him.
verse.note: The verb is rare and can mean either “to wake up fully” or “to stay awake throughout”. On the second reading the disciples fought off sleep and so saw the glory. Translations and commentators are divided, and the context does not settle it.

verse.text: As the men were parting from him, Peter said to Jesus, “Master, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah.” He did not know what he was saying.
verse.note: The Greek is the ordinary word for a tent or hut. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Israel’s wilderness sanctuary and for the shelters of the Feast of Booths. “Tabernacles” (KJV) now sounds like a special religious object; other versions have “tents”, “shelters” or “dwellings”.

verse.text: While he was saying this, a cloud came and began to overshadow them, and they were afraid as they entered the cloud.
And a voice came from the cloud, saying, “This is my Son, the Chosen One; listen to him!”
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read “the Chosen One” here. Many later manuscripts read “my beloved Son”, which matches the parallel accounts in Matthew and Mark and the voice at Jesus’ baptism. Most scholars think copyists adjusted Luke’s wording to the more familiar form.

verse.text: When the voice had spoken, Jesus was found alone. They kept silent, and in those days they told no one anything of what they had seen.
On the next day, when they had come down from the mountain, a large crowd met him.
And a man from the crowd shouted, “Teacher, I beg you to look at my son, because he is my only child.

text.q: Look, a spirit seizes him, and suddenly he screams; it convulses him until he foams at the mouth, and only with a struggle does it leave him, battering him as it goes.
I begged your disciples to drive it out, but they could not.”

verse.text: Jesus answered, “You faithless and perverse generation! How long will I be with you and put up with you? Bring your son here.”
While the boy was still approaching, the demon threw him to the ground and convulsed him violently. But Jesus rebuked the unclean spirit, healed the boy, and gave him back to his father.
And all were astounded at the majesty of God. While everyone was marveling at everything he was doing, he said to his disciples,

text.q: “Let these words sink into your ears: the Son of Man is about to be handed over into human hands.”

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary word for transferring someone into another’s custody or power. The Gospels use the same word for what Judas, the priests and Pilate each do to Jesus, so one rendering is kept throughout to let that chain be seen. Most versions have “delivered” or “betrayed” here.

verse.text: But they did not understand this saying; it was veiled from them so that they would not perceive it, and they were afraid to ask him about this saying.
A dispute arose among them as to which of them was the greatest.
verse.note: The same Greek word appears in the next verse as “reasoning”. It can mean an open argument or an inward thought, and the phrase could also be read as “a thought entered them”. On that reading the disciples never voiced the question, and Jesus answered what they were privately thinking.

verse.text: But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a little child, stood the child beside him,

and said to them, “Whoever welcomes this little child in my name welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me. For the one who is least among all of you—that is the one who is great.”
John responded, “Master, we saw someone driving out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow along with us.”
But Jesus said to him, “Do not stop him, for whoever is not against you is for you.”
As the days drew to their completion for him to be taken up, he set his face to go to Jerusalem,

note.term: for him to be taken up

verse.note: The noun occurs only here in the New Testament. The related verb is used of Jesus’ ascension in Acts and of Elijah’s being taken up in the Greek Old Testament. Most scholars take it to refer to the ascension, probably as the end point of the whole sequence of death, resurrection and exaltation; a few take it simply as a term for his death. This verse begins the long journey to Jerusalem that occupies the next ten chapters of Luke.

verse.text: and he sent messengers ahead of him. They went and entered a Samaritan village to make preparations for him;
but the people did not welcome him, because his face was set toward Jerusalem.

note.term: because his face was set toward Jerusalem

verse.note: Samaritans worshiped on Mount Gerizim and rejected the Jerusalem temple, and relations with Jews were hostile. Jewish pilgrims passing through Samaria on the way to Jerusalem could expect a cold or even violent reception. The request of James and John in the next verse recalls Elijah calling down fire in 2 Kings 1.

verse.text: When the disciples James and John saw this, they said, “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?”
But he turned and rebuked them.

note.term: But he turned and rebuked them.

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add to verse 54 “as Elijah did”, and expand verses 55–56 with “and said, ‘You do not know what kind of spirit you belong to; for the Son of Man did not come to destroy people’s lives but to save them.’” These words are absent from the earliest and best manuscripts, and most scholars regard them as later additions.

verse.text: And they went on to another village.
As they were going along the road, someone said to him, “I will follow you wherever you go.”
Jesus said to him, “Foxes have dens and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”
To another he said, “Follow me.” But he said, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.”
But Jesus said to him, “Leave the dead to bury their own dead; but you, go and announce the kingdom of God everywhere.”

note.term: Leave the dead to bury their own dead

verse.note: Burying a parent was among the most sacred duties in Jewish life and took precedence over almost every other religious obligation. The saying would have sounded shocking, and that is its point: the claim of the kingdom outranks even this. The first “dead” is usually taken figuratively, of those who do not respond to the kingdom, though the exact sense is debated.

verse.text: Yet another said, “I will follow you, Lord; but first let me say goodbye to those at my home.”
But Jesus said, “No one who puts a hand to the plow and keeps looking back is fit for the kingdom of God.”
After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others as well and sent them out two by two ahead of him into every town and place where he himself was about to go.
verse.note: The manuscripts are closely divided between “seventy-two” and “seventy,” here and in verse 17, and both readings are early. The Greek text followed here prints “seventy-two”; many English versions read “seventy.” Either number may echo a traditional count of the world’s nations, but that connection is uncertain.

verse.text: He said to them, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. So ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest.

text.q: Go! Look, I am sending you out like lambs among wolves.
Do not carry a purse or a bag or sandals, and greet no one along the road.
Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house.’
And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; but if not, it will return to you.

verse.note: “Son of” is a Semitic idiom for someone characterized by or belonging to a thing, so “a son of peace” is a person disposed to peace and ready to receive the greeting. Some translations paraphrase it as “a peaceful person” or “someone who promotes peace.” The idiom is kept here because the Greek keeps it.

text.q: Stay in that same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the worker deserves his wages. Do not move around from house to house.
And whatever town you enter where they welcome you, eat what is set before you,
heal the sick who are in it, and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’
But whatever town you enter where they do not welcome you, go out into its streets and say,
‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Yet know this: the kingdom of God has come near.’
I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.
Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the deeds of power done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have turned back long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.

verse.note: The Greek is the ordinary word for “power,” used in the plural for acts that display it. The same word appears as “power” in verse 19, and this rendering keeps that link visible. There is no dispute about the meaning, and “miracles” is an equally acceptable translation.

Most translations have “repented,” which in modern English centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, and sackcloth and ashes were the outward signs of it. “Repent” remains the standard rendering and is understood by many readers to include a change of life.

text.q: But it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon at the judgment than for you.
And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? You will be brought down to Hades.
Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me; and whoever rejects me rejects the one who sent me.”

verse.text: The seventy-two returned with joy, saying, “Lord, even the demons submit to us in your name!”
He said to them, “I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven.

text.q: Look, I have given you the authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing will harm you at all.
Yet do not rejoice in this, that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names have been written in the heavens.”

verse.note: The Greek is plural here, a Semitic turn of phrase for God’s dwelling, while verses 15, 18 and 21 use the singular. Most translations flatten the plural to “heaven.” The image is of a heavenly register in which the names of God’s people are recorded.

verse.text: At that very hour he exulted in the Holy Spirit and said, “I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for this was your good pleasure.

text.q: All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.”

verse.text: Then turning to the disciples, he said privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see!

text.q: For I tell you that many prophets and kings wanted to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.”

verse.text: Just then an expert in the law stood up to put him to the test, saying, “Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
verse.note: Many translations have “lawyer,” which now suggests an attorney who represents clients in court. The word names a man learned in the Law of Moses and its interpretation, a group overlapping with those the Gospels call scribes. Several modern versions also use “expert in the law.”

The adjective comes from the word for “age,” and in Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, a matter of kind as well as length. The man is asking how to have a share in that coming age. “Eternal” is the standard rendering and is kept here.

verse.text: He said to him, “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?”
He answered, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.’”
He said to him, “You have answered correctly. Do this, and you will live.”
But he, wanting to justify himself, said to Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?”
Jesus took up the question and said, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among bandits, who stripped him, beat him, and went away, leaving him half dead.
verse.note: Greek distinguishes this word from the one for a thief who steals by stealth; it denotes armed, violent men who plunder travelers, often in gangs. Most translations have “robbers,” which is not wrong but can suggest a burglar or mugger. The steep desert road from Jerusalem down to Jericho was known for such attacks.

text.q: Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side.
In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a Samaritan who was traveling came to where he was, and when he saw him he was moved with compassion.

verse.note: Jews and Samaritans had a long history of religious and ethnic hostility, and each regarded the other’s worship as illegitimate. After a priest and a Levite, hearers would likely have expected an ordinary Israelite as the third traveler. Making a Samaritan the one who helps is the shock of the story.

text.q: He went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
The next day he took out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’

verse.note: A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s pay for a laborer. Two denarii would have covered a number of days’ board at an inn, though exactly how many is uncertain.

text.q: Which of these three do you think became a neighbor to the man who fell among the bandits?”

verse.text: He said, “The one who showed him mercy.” Jesus said to him, “Go, and you do the same.”
As they went on their way, he entered a village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him.
She had a sister called Mary, who sat down at the feet of Jesus and was listening to his word.
verse.note: To sit at a teacher’s feet was the posture of a disciple receiving instruction; Paul uses the same expression of his training under Gamaliel in Acts 22:3. Mary is taking the place of a pupil, not merely sitting nearby. Some manuscripts read “the Lord’s feet” here.

verse.text: But Martha was distracted by all the serving. She came up and said, “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to do the serving alone? So tell her to help me.”
But the Lord answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,

text.q: but few things are needed—or only one. For Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

note.term: but few things are needed—or only one

verse.note: The manuscripts differ here. Many, followed by most English translations, read simply “but one thing is necessary”; others, including some early witnesses and the Greek text translated here, have the longer form “few things are needed, or one.” In the longer form “few things” may refer first to dishes for the meal before the saying narrows to the one thing that matters; which reading is original is disputed.

verse.text: Once he was praying in a certain place, and when he had finished, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.”
He said to them, “When you pray, say: ‘Father, may your name be held holy. May your kingdom come.

note.term: may your name be held holy

verse.note: Traditionally “hallowed be your name,” using an English verb now rarely met elsewhere. The Greek verb is built on the ordinary word for “holy” and, with God’s name as its object, means to treat or acknowledge as holy. The meaning is not in dispute; the choice of English is one of clarity.

note.traditional: Our Father which art in heaven

verse.note: Luke’s form of the prayer is shorter than Matthew’s. Many later manuscripts expand it to match Matthew, reading “Our Father in the heavens” and adding “may your will be done” and “rescue us from the evil one.” The earliest witnesses have the short form translated here, and most scholars regard the longer readings as harmonizations.

text.q: Give us each day our daily bread.

verse.note: The Greek adjective is almost unknown outside the Lord’s Prayer, and its meaning is genuinely uncertain. The main proposals are “for the coming day,” “necessary for existence,” and “for today.” The traditional “daily” is kept because no alternative is secure; most translations do the same and give the other options in a footnote.

text.q: And forgive us our sins, for we ourselves forgive everyone who is indebted to us. And do not bring us into testing.’”

verse.note: Traditionally “temptation.” In the usage of the period, including the Greek Old Testament, the word mainly means a putting to the proof, an ordeal that shows whether someone will stay faithful; modern “temptation” has narrowed to enticement to sin and can suggest that God lures people into wrongdoing. Lexicons recognize both senses and scholars disagree about which is in view here, so this is an editorial choice. Most versions keep “temptation,” and some have “time of trial.”

verse.text: Then he said to them, “Suppose one of you has a friend and goes to him at midnight and says to him, ‘Friend, lend me three loaves,

text.q: for a friend of mine has arrived at my house from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him.’
And suppose he answers from inside, ‘Do not bother me. The door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed. I cannot get up and give you anything.’
I tell you, even if he will not get up and give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his shamelessness he will get up and give him as much as he needs.

verse.note: Traditionally “importunity” or “persistence.” In the usage of the period the word means lack of shame, brazenness, and there is little evidence that it meant persistence as such; the petitioner is shameless in knocking at midnight. Some scholars instead refer “his” to the man in bed, who acts to avoid being shamed, but most take it of the one asking.

text.q: And I tell you: ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.
For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.
Which of you fathers, if his son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead of a fish?
Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion?
If you then, evil as you are, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!”

verse.text: Now he was driving out a demon that was mute. When the demon had gone out, the man who had been mute spoke, and the crowds were amazed.
But some of them said, “It is by Beelzebul, the ruler of the demons, that he drives out the demons.”
Others, testing him, kept seeking from him a sign from heaven.
But he, knowing their thoughts, said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and house falls upon house.

note.traditional: a house divided against a house falleth

verse.note: The Greek is terse and can be read two ways: houses collapsing onto one another, as a picture of a kingdom laid waste, or “a house divided against a house falls,” matching the parallel sayings in Matthew and Mark. The translation takes the first, which follows the Greek wording more simply; a number of versions take the second.

text.q: And if Satan too is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For you say that I drive out the demons by Beelzebul.
But if I drive out the demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons drive them out? Therefore they themselves will be your judges.
But if it is by the finger of God that I drive out the demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.
When the strong man, fully armed, guards his own estate, his possessions are left in peace.
But when someone stronger than he comes against him and overpowers him, he takes away the full armor on which he had relied and distributes his spoils.
Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters.
When the unclean spirit goes out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none, it says, ‘I will return to my house that I came out of.’
And when it comes, it finds the house swept and put in order.
Then it goes and brings along seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they go in and settle there. And the last state of that person becomes worse than the first.”

verse.text: As he was saying these things, a woman in the crowd raised her voice and said to him, “Blessed is the womb that carried you, and the breasts that nursed you!”
But he said, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and keep it.”
As the crowds were growing larger, he began to say, “This generation is an evil generation. It seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.

text.q: For just as Jonah became a sign to the Ninevites, so the Son of Man will be to this generation.

The queen of the South will be raised at the judgment with the men of this generation and will condemn them, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and look—something greater than Solomon is here.
The men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment with this generation and will condemn it, because they turned back at the proclamation of Jonah, and look—something greater than Jonah is here.

verse.note: Traditionally “repented.” “Repent” now centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek verb in the Gospels carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct—which is what the people of Nineveh do in the book of Jonah. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term understood to include a change of life.

text.q: No one lights a lamp and puts it in a cellar or under a basket, but on the lampstand, so that those who come in may see the light.
Your eye is the lamp of the body. When your eye is generous, your whole body is full of light; but when it is evil, your body is full of darkness.

verse.note: Traditionally “single” or, in modern versions, “healthy.” The Greek word means single or sound, but its opposite in this saying, an “evil” eye, was a known Jewish idiom for stinginess, so the good eye is taken here as a generous one. Most translations keep the physical image with “healthy” and mention generosity in a footnote, and in Luke’s setting, where the subject is how people respond to Jesus, many interpreters think soundness or sincerity is the main point.

text.q: See to it, then, that the light in you is not darkness.
If then your whole body is full of light, with no part of it dark, it will be full of light all over, as when the lamp shines on you with its brightness.”

verse.text: When he had finished speaking, a Pharisee asked him to have a meal with him, so he went in and reclined at the table.
The Pharisee was amazed when he saw that he did not first wash before the meal.
verse.note: The Greek verb is the one usually rendered “baptize”; here it has its ordinary sense of immersing or washing. The issue is not hygiene but the ritual washing before meals that Pharisees observed as part of their purity tradition.

verse.text: But the Lord said to him, “Now you Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and the dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness.

text.q: Fools! Did not the one who made the outside make the inside as well?
But give what is inside as charity, and look—everything is clean for you.

note.term: give what is inside as charity
note.traditional: give alms of such things as ye have

verse.note: The Greek is compressed and its sense is disputed. It may mean giving the contents of cup and dish to the poor, or giving from what is within oneself, that is, from the heart; some take it as “give what you have.” The translation leaves the phrase as open as the Greek.

text.q: But woe to you Pharisees! For you tithe mint and rue and every garden herb, yet you pass over justice and the love of God. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.
Woe to you Pharisees! For you love the seat of honor in the synagogues and the greetings in the marketplaces.
Woe to you! For you are like unmarked tombs, and the people who walk over them do not know it.”

verse.note: Under the Law, contact with a grave made a person ritually unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16), so burial places were marked to warn passersby. The charge is that the Pharisees, who prized purity, spread defilement to people who never notice it.

verse.text: One of the experts in the law answered him, “Teacher, in saying these things you insult us too.”
verse.note: Traditionally “lawyers.” The word names specialists in the Law of Moses and its interpretation, a group overlapping with the scribes; “lawyer” now suggests an attorney representing clients in court. Several modern versions use “expert in the law” or something close to it, while others keep “lawyer.”

verse.text: He said, “Woe to you experts in the law as well! For you load people with burdens hard to carry, and you yourselves do not touch the burdens with one of your fingers.

text.q: Woe to you! For you build the tombs of the prophets, and it was your ancestors who killed them.
So you are witnesses and approve of the deeds of your ancestors: they killed them, and you do the building.
For this reason the Wisdom of God also said, ‘I will send them prophets and apostles, and some of them they will kill and persecute,’

verse.note: No such saying is found in the Jewish Scriptures or in any other surviving text. It may come from a lost writing, or “the Wisdom of God” may be a way of speaking of God’s purpose or of Jesus himself; in Matthew’s parallel Jesus speaks the words in his own person. It is also uncertain where the quotation ends; the translation closes it at the end of this verse.

text.q: so that this generation may be called to account for the blood of all the prophets poured out since the foundation of the world,
from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who perished between the altar and the sanctuary. Yes, I tell you, this generation will be called to account for it.

note.term: from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah

verse.note: Abel is the first person murdered in Scripture (Genesis 4). Zechariah is usually identified with the priest stoned in the temple court in 2 Chronicles 24:20–22. In the traditional Hebrew ordering of the books Chronicles stands last, so the two names would span the whole of Scripture, though that ordering cannot be proved for the first century.

text.q: Woe to you experts in the law! For you have taken away the key of knowledge. You did not go in yourselves, and you hindered those who were going in.”

verse.text: When he went out from there, the scribes and the Pharisees began to oppose him fiercely and to question him closely about many things,
lying in wait to catch him in something he said.

Meanwhile, when a crowd of many thousands had gathered, so that they were trampling one another, he began to speak to his disciples first: “Be on your guard against the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.
verse.note: The Greek word for “first” stands between the mention of the disciples and the opening of the speech, and can attach to either. Here it is taken with what precedes: Jesus speaks to his disciples first and to the crowd later (verses 15 and 54). The alternative, followed by some translations, is “First of all, be on your guard.”

text.q: Nothing is covered up that will not be uncovered, and nothing hidden that will not be made known.
Therefore whatever you have said in the dark will be heard in the light, and what you have whispered in the inner rooms will be proclaimed on the housetops.
I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do.
But I will show you whom to fear: fear the one who, after killing, has authority to throw into Gehenna. Yes, I tell you, fear that one.

verse.note: Gehenna is a place name: the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which by the first century had become a name for the place of final punishment. Most English translations render it “hell,” often with a footnote giving the name. The name is kept here because “hell” merges Gehenna with Hades, the realm of the dead, and with much later imagery.

text.q: Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Yet not one of them is forgotten in the sight of God.

verse.note: The coin is the assarion, a small copper coin worth one-sixteenth of a denarius, the usual day’s wage for a laborer. Small birds like these were sold cheaply as food. The “tiny coin” of verse 59 is the lepton, the smallest coin in circulation, worth one-eighth of an assarion.

text.q: But even the hairs of your head have all been counted. Do not fear; you are worth more than many sparrows.
I tell you, everyone who acknowledges me before people, the Son of Man will also acknowledge before the angels of God;
but whoever denies me in the sight of people will be denied in the sight of the angels of God.
And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.
When they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not worry about how or what you will answer in your defense, or what you will say,
for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you must say.”

verse.text: Someone in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.”
But he said to him, “Man, who appointed me judge or divider over you?”
Then he said to them, “Watch out, and guard yourselves against every kind of greed, because even when someone has more than enough, his life does not come from his possessions.”
And he told them a parable: “The land of a certain rich man produced a good crop.

text.q: And he reasoned to himself, ‘What shall I do, since I have nowhere to store my crops?’
And he said, ‘This is what I will do: I will tear down my barns and build bigger ones, and there I will store all my grain and my goods,
and I will say to my soul, “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, enjoy yourself.”’
But God said to him, ‘Fool! This very night your soul is being demanded back from you. And the things you have prepared—whose will they be?’

verse.note: The Greek word means both a person’s life and the inner self. It is rendered “soul” in verses 19–20, where the rich man addresses himself, and “life” in verses 22–23, but it is one word throughout, and “For this reason” in verse 22 builds on that link. Several modern translations have “your life is being demanded” here.

text.q: So it is with the one who stores up treasure for himself and is not rich toward God.”

verse.text: Then he said to his disciples, “For this reason I tell you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear.

text.q: For life is more than food, and the body more than clothing.
Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storeroom nor barn, and yet God feeds them. How much more you are worth than the birds!
And which of you by worrying can add a cubit to the length of his life?

note.term: a cubit to the length of his life
note.traditional: add one cubit to his stature

verse.note: The Greek noun can mean either age (length of life) or bodily height, and a cubit is a measure of length, about eighteen inches. The older tradition has “add a cubit to his stature”; most modern translations take it as a figure for adding a short stretch to one’s lifespan. That reading suits verse 26, which calls this “the smallest thing,” as an extra eighteen inches of height would not be.

text.q: If then you cannot do even the smallest thing, why do you worry about the rest?
Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin. Yet I tell you, not even Solomon in all his glory was dressed like one of these.
But if God so clothes the grass, which is in the field today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, you of little faith!
And you, do not seek what you will eat and what you will drink, and do not be anxious,

verse.note: This verb occurs only here in the New Testament, and it is a different word from the one rendered “worry” elsewhere in the passage. In the period it could mean to be lifted up and so arrogant, its usual sense in the Septuagint, or to be in suspense, unsettled, anxious. The context of concern over food and drink favors the second sense, which is the majority view.

text.q: for all the nations of the world seek after these things, and your Father knows that you need them.

verse.note: The Greek word is the one this translation usually renders “Gentiles”; it means peoples or nations, and in the plural often the non-Jewish peoples in particular. “Nations” is used here because the phrase is “all the nations of the world.” The contrast is still between peoples who do not know God and disciples who know him as Father.

text.q: Instead, seek his kingdom, and these things will be added to you.
Do not fear, little flock, for your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom.
Sell your possessions and give alms. Make yourselves purses that do not wear out, an unfailing treasure in the heavens, where no thief comes near and no moth destroys.
For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
Keep your robes belted up and your lamps burning,

verse.note: Literally “let your loins be girded.” A long robe was hitched up and tucked into the belt for work or travel, so the phrase means to be ready for action; many modern translations paraphrase as “be dressed for action.” The image is kept here because the same verb returns in verse 37, where the master belts up his own robe to serve.

text.q: and be like people waiting for their master to come back from the wedding feast, so that when he comes and knocks they can open the door for him at once.
Blessed are those slaves whom the master finds awake when he comes. Truly I tell you, he will belt up his own robe, have them recline at the table, and come and serve them.

verse.note: The Greek word means a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired servant; most English translations soften it to “servants,” though some recent ones have “slaves.” The status gives the saying its force: a master who dresses for work and waits on his own slaves at table reverses every expectation.

text.q: Whether he comes in the second watch or in the third and finds them so, blessed are they.
But know this: if the owner of the house had known at what hour the thief was coming, he would not have let his house be broken into.
You too must be ready, because the Son of Man is coming at an hour when you do not expect him.”

verse.text: Peter said, “Lord, are you telling this parable to us, or to everyone as well?”
And the Lord said, “Who then is the faithful, sensible manager whom the master will put in charge of his household staff, to give out the food ration at the proper time?

text.q: Blessed is that slave whom his master finds doing so when he comes.
I tell you truly, he will put him in charge of all his possessions.
But if that slave says in his heart, ‘My master is taking a long time to come,’ and begins to beat the male and female servants, and to eat and drink and get drunk,
the master of that slave will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and he will cut him in two and assign him his place with the unfaithful.

verse.note: The verb literally means to cut in two, a form of execution known in the ancient world. Because the slave is afterward assigned a place, some take it as a figure for a severe flogging or for being cut off from the household. The translation keeps the literal sense and with it the harshness of the parable.

The Greek word can mean “unfaithful” or “unbelieving,” and many translations have “unbelievers” here. “Unfaithful” is chosen because the parable began by asking who is the “faithful” manager (verse 42), and this is the opposite term from the same word-family. Hearers may well have caught both senses.

text.q: That slave who knew his master’s will and did not get ready or act in accordance with it will be beaten with many blows;

but the one who did not know, and did things deserving of blows, will be beaten with few. From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required, and from the one to whom much has been entrusted, even more will be asked.
I came to throw fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled!

note.term: how I wish it were already kindled

verse.note: The Greek is compressed and its idiom is disputed. Most take it as a wish, as here; the alternative reads a question, “What do I want, if it is already kindled?”, meaning that the fire is already alight. What the fire stands for—judgment, purification, the Spirit, or the division described in verses 51–53—is also debated.

text.q: But I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how hard pressed I am until it is completed!
Do you think that I have come to give peace on the earth? No, I tell you, but rather division.
For from now on five in one house will be divided, three against two and two against three;

they will be divided, father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against her mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.”

note.term: father against son and son against father

verse.note: The list echoes Micah 7:6, where the breakdown of trust within a household marks a time of crisis before God acts. Some Jewish texts associate such family strife with the troubles expected before the end. The saying presents Jesus’ mission as bringing that crisis on.

verse.text: He also said to the crowds, “When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say at once, ‘A rainstorm is coming,’ and so it happens.

text.q: And when you see a south wind blowing, you say, ‘There will be scorching heat,’ and it happens.
Hypocrites! You know how to interpret the face of the earth and the sky, but how is it that you do not know how to interpret this present time?
And why do you not judge for yourselves what is just?

verse.note: Most translations have “what is right.” Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice). “Just” is used here because the saying leads straight into an illustration from the law court, where the point is to settle a claim before the judge does.

text.q: For as you are going with your opponent before a magistrate, make an effort on the way to settle with him, so that he does not drag you before the judge, and the judge hand you over to the bailiff, and the bailiff throw you into prison.
I tell you, you will never get out of there until you have paid back even the last tiny coin.”

verse.text: At that very time some people were present who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices.

note.term: whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices

verse.note: The phrase implies that Pilate’s soldiers killed these Galilean pilgrims while they were offering sacrifices, which could only have happened at the temple in Jerusalem. Neither this incident nor the collapse of the tower in Siloam (verse 4) is recorded in any other surviving source. Both were evidently recent news that Jesus’s hearers knew.

verse.text: He answered them, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans because they have suffered these things?

text.q: No, I tell you; but unless you turn back, you will all perish likewise.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is “repent,” which most translations keep as an established term that includes a change of life. In current English, however, “repent” centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word in the Gospels carries the prophets’ call to “return” to God—a change of direction in mind and conduct—so “turn back” is used here.

text.q: Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them—do you think they were worse debtors than all the other people living in Jerusalem?

verse.note: The Greek word is literally “debtors,” and most translations paraphrase it as “offenders,” “sinners” or “more guilty.” Speaking of sin as a debt owed to God was a common Jewish idiom (compare the Lord’s Prayer), and it is parallel here to “sinners” in verse 2. The image is kept because the Greek has it.

text.q: No, I tell you; but unless you turn back, you will all perish in the same way.”

verse.text: Then he told this parable: “A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came looking for fruit on it and found none.

text.q: So he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have been coming to look for fruit on this fig tree and finding none. Cut it down! Why should it use up the ground as well?’
But he answered him, ‘Sir, leave it this year too, until I dig around it and put manure on it.
Then if it bears fruit in the coming year—but if not, you can cut it down.’”

note.term: Then if it bears fruit in the coming year—but if not
note.traditional: if it bears fruit next year, well and good; but if not

verse.note: The Greek sentence breaks off without stating what happens if the tree bears fruit. Most translations supply “well” or “fine.” The broken sentence is kept here; it is a natural feature of speech, and the unstated outcome is obvious. “In the coming year” could also be rendered more loosely as “in the future.”

verse.text: He was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath.
And there was a woman there who for eighteen years had had a disabling spirit; she was bent over and unable to straighten up fully.
verse.note: The closing Greek phrase can be read with “straighten up” (she could not straighten up completely) or with “unable” (she could not straighten up at all). Interpreters and translations are divided, and the difference is one of degree. The first reading is followed here.

verse.text: When Jesus saw her, he called to her and said, “Woman, you are released from your disability,”
and he laid his hands on her. At once she was made straight, and she began glorifying God.

But the synagogue leader, indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, responded by saying to the crowd, “There are six days on which one ought to work; so come and be healed on those days, and not on the Sabbath day.”
The Lord answered him, “Hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it?

text.q: And this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan has bound for eighteen long years—ought she not to have been untied from this bond on the Sabbath day?”

note.traditional: loosed / set free from this bond

verse.note: Jesus uses the same verb for untying an ox or donkey (verse 15) and for releasing the woman, and sets it against Satan’s having “bound” her. Most modern translations have “untie” in verse 15 and “set free” here, which hides the repetition on which the argument turns. Likewise “ought” here answers the synagogue leader’s “ought” in verse 14, as it does in the Greek.

verse.text: As he said these things, all his opponents were put to shame, and the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things being done by him.
So he said, “What is the kingdom of God like, and to what shall I compare it?

text.q: It is like a mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden; it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the sky nested in its branches.”

note.term: the birds of the sky nested in its branches

verse.note: The image of a great tree in whose branches the birds nest is used in the Scriptures for a kingdom that shelters many nations (Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6; Daniel 4:12, 21). Hearers familiar with those passages would have caught the echo. Mustard is a garden herb that grows unusually large from a very small seed; calling it a “tree” serves that echo.

verse.text: And again he said, “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God?

text.q: It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until all of it was leavened.”

verse.note: The measure is the saton (Hebrew seah). Three of them come to roughly forty liters of flour, enough bread for well over a hundred people. The quantity is deliberately enormous, matching the tree that grows from the mustard seed. “Leaven” was a piece of fermented dough kept back from an earlier batch, not packaged yeast.

verse.text: He went on through town after town and village after village, teaching and making his way to Jerusalem.
Someone said to him, “Lord, are only a few being saved?” He said to them,

text.q: “Strive to enter through the narrow door, because many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able,

once the master of the house has risen and shut the door and you begin to stand outside and knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open up for us!’ And he will answer you, ‘I do not know you, or where you are from.’

note.term: once the master of the house has risen

verse.note: The Greek syntax across verses 24–25 is loose. The edition translated here links the clause to verse 24: many will be unable to enter once the door has been shut. Many translations instead begin a new sentence at verse 25 (“When once the master of the house has risen … then you will begin to say …”). The overall sense is little affected.

text.q: Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’
But he will say to you, ‘I do not know where you are from. Get away from me, all you workers of wrongdoing!’
In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but yourselves being thrown out.
And people will come from east and west and from north and south and will recline at table in the kingdom of God.
And look, there are some who are last who will be first, and some who are first who will be last.”

verse.text: At that very hour some Pharisees came up and said to him, “Leave and go on from here, because Herod wants to kill you.”
He said to them, “Go and tell that fox, ‘Look, I am casting out demons and performing healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I reach my goal.’
verse.note: Herod here is Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee and Perea who had executed John the Baptist. In Greek and Jewish usage the fox was a figure for craftiness, and sometimes for a petty creature in contrast to a lion. Which nuance dominates here is debated; either way the term is dismissive.

Older versions have “I shall be perfected”; modern ones vary between “I finish my course,” “I reach my goal” and similar. The verb means to be brought to an intended end or completion, not to become morally flawless. Most interpreters take it as pointing to Jesus’s death in Jerusalem (verse 33). “Today and tomorrow, and on the third day” is an idiom for a short, fixed period.

text.q: Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day after, because it cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem.
Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her—how often I wanted to gather your children the way a hen gathers her own brood under her wings, and you did not want it!
Look, your house is left to you. And I tell you, you will certainly not see me until the time comes when you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!’”

note.term: your house is left to you
note.traditional: your house is left to you desolate

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add “desolate,” probably under the influence of Jeremiah 22:5 or the parallel in Matthew 23:38 as commonly read. The earliest witnesses to Luke lack the word, and it is omitted here. “Your house” may refer to the temple or to the city and its people as a whole; the saying means it is abandoned to its own keeping.

verse.text: One Sabbath, when he went into the house of one of the leaders of the Pharisees to eat bread, they were watching him closely.
verse.note: “To eat bread” is a Semitic idiom for having a meal, not a description of the menu. The literal wording is kept because the guest's exclamation in verse 15 uses the same phrase for the feast in the kingdom of God.

verse.text: And there in front of him was a man who had dropsy.
verse.note: Dropsy is the older name for edema, a visible swelling of the body caused by retained fluid. It is a symptom of serious underlying illness and not a disease in itself. The Greek term is a standard medical word of the period and occurs only here in the New Testament.

verse.text: Jesus responded by asking the experts in the law and the Pharisees, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath, or not?”
verse.note: The word names men learned in the Law of Moses and its interpretation, a group overlapping with the scribes. “Lawyer,” kept by the KJV, ESV and NRSV, suggests to a modern reader an attorney who represents clients in court. The NIV and several other recent versions also use “expert in the law.”

verse.text: But they kept silent. So he took hold of the man, cured him, and sent him away.
Then he said to them, “If one of you has a son or an ox that falls into a well, will you not immediately pull him out on the Sabbath day?”
verse.note: Manuscripts differ here: some read “a donkey or an ox,” and a few read “a sheep.” “Son” has strong early support and is the harder reading, since copyists would more readily change it to an animal to match “ox” than the reverse. Most modern editions and translations read “son” or “child.”

verse.text: And they were not able to give an answer to this.
Noticing how those who had been invited were choosing the places of honor, he told them a parable, saying to them,
verse.note: At formal meals guests reclined on couches arranged around the table, and the positions were ranked, with the places nearest the host carrying the most prestige. The Greek word means literally the “first reclining place.” The verbs in verses 8, 10 and 15 are accordingly translated “recline,” where older versions have “sit.”

text.q: “When you are invited by someone to a wedding feast, do not recline in the place of honor, in case someone more distinguished than you has been invited by him,
and the one who invited both you and him will come and say to you, ‘Give your place to this person,’ and then in shame you will begin to take the last place.

But when you are invited, go and recline in the last place, so that when the one who invited you comes, he will say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher.’ Then you will have honor in the presence of all who are reclining at table with you.
For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.”

verse.text: He also said to the one who had invited him, “When you give a lunch or a dinner, do not invite your friends or your brothers or your relatives or rich neighbors, in case they also invite you in return and you are repaid.

text.q: But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind,
and you will be blessed, because they have no means to repay you; for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.”

verse.text: When one of those reclining at table with him heard this, he said to him, “Blessed is anyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!”
But he said to him, “A man was giving a great dinner, and he invited many people.

text.q: At the hour of the dinner he sent his slave to say to those who had been invited, ‘Come, because everything is now ready.’

verse.note: The Greek word ordinarily means a slave, a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. Most English versions since the KJV have “servant,” which softens the social reality a first-century reader would have assumed. The NRSV and some other recent versions also have “slave” here.

text.q: But they all alike began to excuse themselves. The first said to him, ‘I have bought a field, and I must go out and see it. Please have me excused.’
Another said, ‘I have bought five pairs of oxen, and I am on my way to try them out. Please have me excused.’
And another said, ‘I have married a wife, and for that reason I cannot come.’

The slave came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his slave, ‘Go out quickly into the streets and alleys of the city, and bring in here the poor and the crippled and the blind and the lame.’
And the slave said, ‘Master, what you ordered has been done, and there is still room.’
And the master said to the slave, ‘Go out to the roads and hedgerows and compel them to come in, so that my house may be filled.

verse.note: The verb covers both physical force and strong insistence. Here, where a single slave is sent to strangers who would not expect to be invited to such a meal, most interpreters understand urgent persuasion that will not take a polite refusal, and some versions translate “urge” or “make.” The verse was later cited to justify religious coercion, a use the context does not support.

text.q: For I tell you, none of those men who were invited will taste my dinner.’”

verse.note: The “you” is plural in Greek, although the master in the story is speaking to a single slave. Either the master is pictured as addressing his household more broadly, or Jesus here steps out of the parable and speaks directly to his fellow guests, so that “my dinner” becomes his own. The translation keeps the sentence inside the master's speech, as most versions do, but the second reading is widely held.

verse.text: Large crowds were traveling with him, and he turned and said to them,

text.q: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, and yes, even his own life, he cannot be my disciple.

verse.note: In Semitic idiom, “love” and “hate” set side by side can express preference, not emotion: to “hate” one thing is to rank it decisively below another (compare Genesis 29:30–31 and Deuteronomy 21:15). The parallel saying in Matthew 10:37 speaks of loving family “more than me.” The strong word is kept because Luke chose it, and softening it would blunt the saying.

text.q: Whoever does not carry his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple.
For which of you, wanting to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost, to see whether he has enough to complete it?
Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it will begin to mock him,
saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’
Or what king, going out to engage another king in war, will not first sit down and consider whether he is able with ten thousand to meet the one coming against him with twenty thousand?
And if he is not, while the other is still far away he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace.
In the same way, then, anyone among you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.
Salt, then, is good; but if even salt becomes tasteless, with what will it be seasoned?

note.traditional: have lost his savour; has lost its taste

verse.note: The verb elsewhere means “to make foolish” (as in Romans 1:22), and its use of salt here and in Matthew 5:13 is unusual; some scholars suspect a wordplay in an underlying Aramaic saying. Pure salt does not lose its saltiness, and the image is often explained by the impure salt of the region, from which the sodium chloride could leach out and leave a useless residue.

text.q: It is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile; people throw it out. Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

verse.text: Now all the tax collectors and sinners were drawing near to him to listen to him.
And the Pharisees and the scribes were grumbling, saying, “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.”
So he told them this parable:

text.q: “What man among you, having a hundred sheep and losing one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the lost one until he finds it?
And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing,
and when he comes home, he calls together his friends and neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost.’
I tell you that in the same way there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who turns back than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of turning back.

verse.note: The traditional rendering is “repent” and “repentance,” which most translations keep as an established term. In modern English “repent” centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word in the Gospels carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. “Turn back” is used for that reason, and it suits a chapter about the lost being found.

text.q: Or what woman, having ten drachmas, if she loses one drachma, does not light a lamp and sweep the house and search carefully until she finds it?

verse.note: The drachma was a Greek silver coin, roughly equal to a Roman denarius, which was about a day’s wage for a laborer. Ten drachmas would be a modest household’s savings, so losing one was a real loss. Many translations say “silver coins”; the name of the coin is kept here because it is what the Greek says.

text.q: And when she has found it, she calls together her friends and neighbors, saying, ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma that I lost.’
In the same way, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of God’s angels over one sinner who turns back.”

verse.text: Then he said, “A certain man had two sons.

text.q: The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me the share of the property that falls to me.’ So he divided his livelihood between them.

note.term: the share of the property that falls to me

verse.note: Under the Law of Moses the firstborn received a double share (Deuteronomy 21:17), so the younger of two sons could expect one third. An inheritance normally passed at the father’s death; asking for it while he was alive, and then selling it and leaving, would have struck the first hearers as a serious breach of a son’s duty.

text.q: Not many days later, the younger son gathered everything together and traveled to a distant country, and there he squandered his property by living recklessly.

verse.note: The adverb describes a life that is wasteful and out of control. It can mean simply extravagant spending or can imply moral dissipation; the Greek does not specify, and the charge about prostitutes in verse 30 comes from the older brother, not the narrator. The traditional title “Prodigal Son” reflects this word.

text.q: When he had spent everything, a severe famine came over that country, and he began to be in need.
So he went and attached himself to one of the citizens of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed pigs.

verse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the Law of Moses, and Jews did not keep them. The detail tells the hearer that the son is in Gentile territory and has sunk as low as a Jewish audience could imagine.

text.q: He longed to fill his belly with the carob pods that the pigs were eating, and no one gave him anything.

verse.note: Manuscripts divide here. The SBLGNT, translated here, reads “fill his belly with”; other early manuscripts, followed by some critical editions and translations, read “be satisfied with” or “be fed with.” The sense is little affected. The pods are those of the carob tree, used as animal fodder and eaten by the very poor.

text.q: But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired workers have more than enough bread, and here I am perishing of hunger!
I will get up and go to my father and say to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you;

verse.note: “Heaven” here is a reverent Jewish way of referring to God without naming him. The son is confessing that he has sinned against God and against his father.

text.q: I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired workers.”’
So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and he ran and threw his arms around his neck and kissed him.
The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
But the father said to his slaves, ‘Quickly, bring out the best robe and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet,

verse.note: Most English versions say “servants,” but the Greek word denotes people who were owned, not employed. The parable distinguishes three groups: the household slaves here, the “hired workers” of verses 17 and 19 who were day laborers with the least security, and the “servants” of verse 26, a different and more general Greek word. The related verb appears in the older son’s complaint in verse 29, rendered “slaving.”

text.q: and bring the fattened calf, slaughter it, and let us eat and celebrate,
because this son of mine was dead and has come back to life; he was lost and has been found.’ And they began to celebrate.
Now his older son was in the field, and as he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing.
He called over one of the servants and asked what this might mean.
He told him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has slaughtered the fattened calf, because he has gotten him back safe and sound.’
But he became angry and refused to go in. So his father came out and began pleading with him.

But he answered his father, ‘Look, all these years I have been slaving for you, and I never disobeyed a command of yours, yet you never gave me even a young goat so that I could celebrate with my friends.
But when this son of yours came, who has devoured your livelihood with prostitutes, you slaughtered the fattened calf for him!’
He said to him, ‘Child, you are always with me, and everything that is mine is yours.

verse.note: Most translations have “Son” here, but the Greek is not the word for “son” used throughout the parable. It is a different word, “child,” used as an affectionate form of address. The father answers the older son’s anger with tenderness.

text.q: But we had to celebrate and rejoice, because this brother of yours was dead and has come to life, and was lost and has been found.’”

verse.text: He also said to the disciples, “There was a rich man who had a manager, and this manager was accused to him of squandering his property.
verse.note: The word names the agent who ran a wealthy man’s estate and could make binding contracts in his name. “Steward” is the traditional rendering, but it now suggests a ship or a wine waiter; most modern versions use “manager”. The related words in verses 2–4 are rendered “management” and “be manager” to keep the repetition.

text.q: So he called him and said to him, ‘What is this I hear about you? Hand over the account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’
The manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, now that my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg.
I know what I will do, so that when I am removed from the management people will welcome me into their homes.’
And he summoned each one of his master’s debtors. He said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’
He said, ‘A hundred measures of olive oil.’ The manager told him, ‘Take your bill, sit down quickly, and write fifty.’

verse.note: The Greek names two different Hebrew units: the bath, a liquid measure, for the oil, and the cor, a dry measure, for the wheat in verse 7. Estimates of their size vary, but a hundred baths was several thousand liters of oil and a hundred cors was many tons of grain. These are large commercial debts, and the reductions are worth a great deal.

text.q: Then he said to another, ‘And you, how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred measures of wheat.’ He told him, ‘Take your bill and write eighty.’
And the master praised the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly; for the sons of this age are shrewder in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light.

verse.note: The Greek word can mean the manager’s master, as in verses 3 and 5, or “the Lord”, meaning Jesus. Most interpreters take it as the master inside the story, with Jesus’ own comment beginning at “for the sons of this age” or at verse 9. On the other reading the parable ends at verse 7 and this sentence is Luke’s report that Jesus praised the manager.

The word is a time-word: “this age” is the present era, contrasted in Jewish thought with the age to come. “Sons of” is a Semitic idiom for people who belong to something, here set against “sons of light”. Older versions have “world”; several modern versions already have “age”.

text.q: And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of dishonest wealth, so that when it gives out they will welcome you into the eternal tents.

verse.note: The Greek borrows an Aramaic word for money or property; “mammon” is not the name of a god, though Jesus speaks of it in verse 13 as a rival master. The phrase is literally “wealth of unrighteousness”, using the same word that describes the manager in verse 8. It may mean wealth gained dishonestly, but many scholars take it as wealth that belongs to this unjust age, hence “worldly wealth” in some versions.

The Greek word is the ordinary one for a tent, and most versions generalize it here to “dwellings” or “homes”. The plain image is kept because it is striking: a tent is temporary, yet these belong to the age to come and last. “They” who do the welcoming may be the friends made by generosity, or it may be a reverent way of saying that God will welcome.

text.q: Whoever is faithful in very little is faithful also in much, and whoever is dishonest in very little is dishonest also in much.
So if you have not been faithful with dishonest wealth, who will trust you with true wealth?
And if you have not been faithful with what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?
No household slave can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and wealth.”

verse.note: The word means a slave belonging to a household, and the verb rendered “serve” is the one for serving as a slave. Since a slave was owned outright, belonging to two masters is impossible in a way that working two jobs is not. Most versions have “servant”, and some have “slave”.

verse.text: The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, were listening to all this, and they sneered at him.
And he said to them, “You are the ones who justify yourselves before people, but God knows your hearts; for what is exalted among people is an abomination before God.

text.q: The Law and the Prophets were until John; since then the good news of the kingdom of God is being proclaimed, and everyone is forcing their way into it.

note.term: everyone is forcing their way into it
note.traditional: every man presseth into it / everyone forces his way into it

verse.note: The verb can be read as active in sense, as here, or as passive: “everyone is urgently pressed to enter it”. Both readings have scholarly support, and the similar saying in Matthew 11:12 is disputed in the same way. On either reading the point is that John’s arrival marks a new stage in which the kingdom is being announced.

text.q: But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of a letter in the Law to fall.
Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.
There was a rich man who dressed in purple and fine linen and feasted in splendor every day.
And a poor man named Lazarus had been laid at his gate, covered with sores
and longing to eat his fill of what fell from the rich man’s table. Even the dogs would come and lick his sores.
The time came when the poor man died and was carried away by the angels to Abraham’s side. The rich man also died and was buried.

verse.note: The word means the chest or lap, or the fold of a garment over it. To be at someone’s chest was to recline next to them at a banquet, the place of honor and closeness, as in John 13:23. The beggar who longed for table scraps is given the best seat beside Abraham; “side” is the usual modern rendering of this image.

text.q: And in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.
And he called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am in agony in this flame.’
But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that you received your good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise the bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in agony.
And besides all this, a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who want to cross from here to you cannot, and no one may cross from there to us.’
He said, ‘Then I ask you, father, to send him to my father’s house—
for I have five brothers—to warn them, so that they too will not come to this place of torment.’
But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them listen to them.’
He said, ‘No, father Abraham; but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will turn back.’

verse.note: “Repent” now centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, which here would mean the brothers changing how they live. Most translations keep “repent” as an established term understood to include a change of life.

text.q: He said to him, ‘If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.’”

verse.text: He said to his disciples, “It is impossible for stumbling blocks not to come, but woe to the one through whom they come!

text.q: It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea than that he should cause one of these little ones to stumble.
Be on your guard. If your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he turns back, forgive him.

verse.note: The Greek verb carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. “Repent” now suggests mainly feeling sorry, so this translation uses “turn back.” Most translations keep “repent” as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

text.q: And if he sins against you seven times in a day and seven times comes back to you saying, ‘I turn back,’ you must forgive him.”

verse.text: The apostles said to the Lord, “Increase our faith.”
The Lord said, “If you had faith like a mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.

text.q: Which of you who has a slave plowing or tending sheep will say to him when he comes in from the field, ‘Come at once and recline at the table’?

verse.note: The Greek word means a person owned by a master, not a hired worker, and the parable depends on that: a slave who does what he is told has earned no special thanks. The KJV, ESV and NIV have “servant”; the NRSV, NASB and NET have “slave.”

text.q: Will he not say to him instead, ‘Prepare something for my dinner, tie up your tunic and serve me while I eat and drink, and after that you may eat and drink’?
He does not thank the slave for doing what was commanded, does he?
So you also, when you have done everything that was commanded you, say, ‘We are unworthy slaves; we have done what we were obliged to do.’”

verse.note: The Greek adjective ordinarily means “useless” or “worthless.” Here it is usually taken as a statement of modesty: slaves who have only done their duty have no claim to special credit. Translations vary among “unprofitable,” “unworthy” and “worthless”; some scholars propose “to whom nothing is owed,” which fits the parable but is less certain as a meaning of the word.

verse.text: On the way to Jerusalem, he was passing between Samaria and Galilee.

note.traditional: through the midst of Samaria and Galilee
