verse.note: The Greek phrase could mean “through the middle of Samaria and Galilee” or “along the border between” them. Samaria lies south of Galilee, so a route along the border region makes better geographical sense for someone heading to Jerusalem, and it would explain a group that includes both Jews and a Samaritan. The exact route Luke has in mind is debated.

verse.text: As he was entering a village, ten men with a skin disease met him. They stood at a distance
verse.note: The Greek word names someone with the condition regulated in Leviticus 13–14, a range of scaly skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean, which is why the men are “cleansed.” “Leper” today means a person with Hansen’s disease, which is narrower than the Greek term and may not be included in it. Most translations keep “lepers,” usually with a footnote making this point; the traditional word does convey the severity and social exclusion involved.

verse.text: and raised their voices, saying, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!”
When he saw them, he said to them, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” And as they went, they were cleansed.
verse.note: Under Leviticus 13–14 a person with this condition lived apart from the community, which is why the men stand at a distance, and could return only after a priest had examined them and declared them clean. Jesus sends them for that inspection before any change is visible; the cleansing comes as they go.

verse.text: One of them, seeing that he had been healed, returned, glorifying God in a loud voice,
and fell on his face at the feet of Jesus, thanking him. And he was a Samaritan.
Jesus responded, “Were not the ten cleansed? Where are the nine?

text.q: Was no one found returning to give glory to God except this foreigner?”

verse.note: Samaritans worshiped the God of Israel and kept the Law of Moses, but Jews regarded them as outsiders. The Greek word used here occurs only this once in the New Testament; it is the term used on the inscription in the Jerusalem temple that warned non-Jews not to enter the inner courts.

verse.text: And he said to him, “Get up and go on your way; your faith has saved you.”
verse.note: The Greek verb means both “heal” and “save,” and many translations have “made you well” here. But all ten were cleansed and only this man is told this, so the saying probably points to more than the cure. The identical sentence closes other scenes in Luke (7:50; 8:48; 18:42).

verse.text: Asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered them, “The kingdom of God is not coming in a way that can be observed,

text.q: nor will they say, ‘Look, here!’ or ‘There!’ For look, the kingdom of God is among you.”

verse.note: The Greek preposition can mean “within” or “among, in the midst of.” “Within you” is the older English rendering, but Jesus is speaking to Pharisees and does not elsewhere describe the kingdom as an inner state, so most recent translations and scholars prefer “among you” or “in your midst.” A third proposal, “within your reach,” also has scholarly support.

verse.text: Then he said to the disciples, “Days will come when you will long to see one of the days of the Son of Man, and you will not see it.

text.q: They will say to you, ‘Look, there! Look, here!’ Do not go off or chase after them.
For just as lightning flashes and lights up the sky from one end to the other, so will the Son of Man be in his day.
But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.
And just as it was in the days of Noah, so it will be also in the days of the Son of Man:
they were eating, drinking, marrying, being given in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark, and the flood came and destroyed them all.
Likewise, just as it was in the days of Lot: they were eating, drinking, buying, selling, planting, building;
but on the day Lot went out from Sodom, it rained fire and sulfur from heaven and destroyed them all.
It will be just the same on the day the Son of Man is revealed.
On that day, anyone on the roof whose belongings are in the house must not go down to take them, and likewise anyone in the field must not turn to what is behind.
Remember Lot’s wife.
Whoever seeks to secure his life will lose it, but whoever loses it will keep it alive.
I tell you, on that night there will be two in one bed: one will be taken and the other left.
There will be two women grinding together: one will be taken and the other left.”

verse.note: Verse 36 (“Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left”) is absent from the earliest and best manuscripts and is not part of the Greek text translated here. It was probably added by copyists from Matthew 24:40. The traditional verse numbers are kept, so the chapter moves from verse 35 to verse 37.

verse.text: They responded and said to him, “Where, Lord?” He said to them, “Where the body is, there the vultures too will gather.”
verse.note: The Greek word normally means “eagle,” and the KJV has “eagles.” Ancient writers did not always distinguish eagles from vultures, and birds gathering at a body are carrion birds, so most modern translations have “vultures.” Some interpreters see an allusion to the eagle standards of the Roman legions; this is possible but uncertain.

verse.text: Then he told them a parable about the need for them to pray always and not lose heart,
saying, “In a certain city there was a judge who neither feared God nor respected any person.

text.q: In that city there was also a widow, and she kept coming to him, saying, ‘Give me justice against my opponent.’
For a time he was unwilling, but afterward he said to himself, ‘Even though I do not fear God or respect any person,
yet because this widow keeps causing me trouble, I will give her justice, so that she will not finally wear me out by her coming.’”

verse.note: The verb literally means to strike someone under the eye, a term from boxing; Paul uses it of disciplining his body in 1 Corinthians 9:27. Most translators take it figuratively here, as “wear me out.” Others think the judge fears, perhaps with grim humor, that the widow will actually come and hit him, or that she will blacken his reputation. The phrase rendered “finally” can also mean “completely” or “continually.”

verse.text: And the Lord said, “Listen to what the unjust judge says.

text.q: Will not God, then, bring about justice for his chosen ones who cry out to him day and night? Will he delay over them?

note.traditional: though he bear long with them (KJV); Will he delay long over them? (RSV, ESV)

verse.note: The Greek is literally “and he is patient over them,” and its connection to the rest of the sentence is disputed. It may be a second question expecting the answer no, as rendered here, or a concession: “even though he is patient with them,” meaning either the chosen ones or their oppressors. A very similar phrase in Sirach 35, in a passage about God hearing the widow’s plea, favors the sense of delay.

text.q: I tell you, he will bring about justice for them quickly. Yet when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on the earth?”

verse.text: He also told this parable to some who were confident in themselves that they were righteous and looked down on the rest:
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice,” “justify” and “vindicate” all render the same group of words. In this chapter the widow’s “justice,” the “unjust” judge, the “unjust” people of the Pharisee’s prayer, those sure they are “righteous,” and the tax collector who goes home “justified” (verse 14) all belong to this group or are closely related to it. Both parables turn on who is truly in the right before God.

text.q: “Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed these words to himself: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of people—grasping, unjust, adulterous—or even like this tax collector.

note.traditional: stood and prayed thus with himself (KJV); standing by himself, prayed thus (ESV, NRSV)

verse.note: The phrase “to himself” can be attached to “prayed” (he prayed silently, or about himself) or to “stood” (he stood by himself, apart from the others). The manuscripts also vary in word order here. With verbs of speaking the phrase normally means “to himself,” which is the reading followed; many modern versions prefer “stood by himself.”

text.q: I fast twice a week; I give a tenth of everything I acquire.’
But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but kept beating his chest and saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, the sinner.’

verse.note: This is not the ordinary word for showing mercy that the blind man uses in verse 38. It belongs to the word-group used for atonement, and in the Septuagint this form appears in prayers asking God to pardon sins; its only other New Testament occurrence is Hebrews 2:17. Spoken in the temple, where atoning sacrifices were offered, the plea asks God to be reconciled to him.

The Greek has the definite article, “the sinner.” Most English versions render “a sinner,” treating the article as generic. It may instead be pointed: the tax collector sees himself as the sinner in the room, while the Pharisee compares himself favorably with everyone else. Grammarians are divided, and either rendering is defensible.

text.q: I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other. For all who exalt themselves will be humbled, but those who humble themselves will be exalted.”

verse.text: People were bringing even their babies to him so that he might touch them, but when the disciples saw this, they rebuked them.
But Jesus called for them, saying, “Let the little children come to me, and do not stop them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.

text.q: Truly I tell you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.”

verse.text: A certain leader asked him, “Good teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
verse.note: Traditionally “ruler,” which suggests a king or prince to a modern reader. The word covers anyone holding a position of authority, such as a magistrate, a synagogue official or a member of a governing council, and Luke does not say which this man was. The familiar description “rich young ruler” combines details from three Gospels; Luke does not call him young.

The word translated “eternal” is related to the word for “age,” and in Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, as verse 30 makes explicit. It describes a kind of life as well as an unending one. “Eternal” is the standard rendering; a minority of translators prefer “life of the age to come.”

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except one—God.

text.q: You know the commandments: ‘Do not commit adultery. Do not murder. Do not steal. Do not give false testimony. Honor your father and mother.’”

verse.text: He said, “All these I have kept since my youth.”
When Jesus heard this, he said to him, “One thing you still lack. Sell everything you have and distribute it to the poor, and you will have treasure in the heavens; then come, follow me.”
verse.note: The Greek is plural here, a Semitic turn of phrase that reflects Hebrew and Aramaic, where the word for heaven is always plural. Most translations flatten it to “heaven.” This translation keeps the plural where the Greek has it for God’s dwelling; in verse 13 the word is singular.

verse.text: But when he heard this he became very sad, for he was extremely rich.
Looking at him, Jesus said, “How hard it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!

text.q: Indeed, it is easier for a camel to enter through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.”

verse.text: Those who heard this said, “Then who can be saved?”
He said, “What is impossible for people is possible for God.”
Then Peter said, “Look, we have left what was ours and followed you.”
He said to them, “Truly I tell you, there is no one who has left house or wife or brothers or parents or children for the sake of the kingdom of God

text.q: who will not receive back many times as much in this present time, and in the age to come eternal life.”

verse.text: Taking the Twelve aside, he said to them, “Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and everything written through the prophets about the Son of Man will be accomplished.

text.q: For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, and he will be mocked and insulted and spat on,

verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural it regularly refers to the non-Jewish peoples and is then translated “Gentiles.” Here it points to the Roman authorities, who carried out the mocking, flogging and execution described.

text.q: and after flogging him they will kill him, and on the third day he will rise.”

verse.text: But they understood none of this; the saying was hidden from them, and they did not grasp what was being said.
As he was approaching Jericho, a blind man was sitting beside the road, begging.
Hearing a crowd going by, he asked what this meant.
They told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by.
And he cried out, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!”
verse.note: “Son of David” was a title for the Messiah, the expected king from David’s line. The blind man’s cry is therefore a public acclamation of Jesus as that king, made as Jesus nears Jerusalem. Luke records no one else addressing Jesus this way.

verse.text: Those who were in front rebuked him, telling him to be silent, but he shouted all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”
Jesus stopped and ordered that he be brought to him. When he came near, Jesus asked him,
“What do you want me to do for you?” He said, “Lord, I want to see again.”
And Jesus said to him, “See again! Your faith has saved you.”

note.traditional: hath saved thee (KJV); has made you well (ESV); has healed you (NIV)

verse.note: The verb means both “heal” or “rescue” and “save,” and it is the same word used in verse 26, “who can be saved?” Many modern versions render “has made you well” or “has healed you” here. “Saved” is kept so that the link is visible; Luke may well intend both the restored sight and something more, since the man at once follows Jesus.

verse.text: Immediately he could see again, and he began to follow him, glorifying God. And all the people, when they saw it, gave praise to God.
He entered Jericho and was passing through.
There was a man there named Zacchaeus; he was a chief tax collector, and he was rich.
He was trying to see who Jesus was, but he could not because of the crowd, for he was short in stature.
So he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore fig tree to see him, because Jesus was about to pass that way.
When he came to the place, Jesus looked up and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.”
So he hurried down and welcomed him with joy.
When they saw it, they all began to grumble, saying, “He has gone in to be the guest of a sinful man.”
But Zacchaeus stood and said to the Lord, “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have extorted anything from anyone, I pay back four times as much.”
verse.note: The Greek verbs “give” and “pay back” are in the present tense. Most interpreters take them as a resolve made on the spot (“I am now giving”), which fits Jesus’ reply that salvation has come “today.” A minority reads them as Zacchaeus’s existing practice, offered in his own defense against the crowd’s grumbling. The plain English present leaves both readings open.

The verb means to squeeze money out of someone by false charges or intimidation, which “defrauded” or “cheated” understates. It is the same verb used in Luke 3:14, where soldiers are told not to do this. Fourfold repayment echoes the heaviest restitution the Law of Moses prescribes for theft.

verse.text: Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham.

text.q: For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost.”

verse.text: As they were listening to this, he went on to tell a parable, because he was near Jerusalem and they supposed that the kingdom of God was about to appear at once.
So he said, “A man of noble birth traveled to a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and then return.
verse.note: Here the word means royal authority, the right to rule as king, not a territory: the nobleman travels to a higher power to be confirmed as king over his own country. Hearers would probably have recalled Archelaus, son of Herod the Great, who went to Rome to have his rule confirmed while a delegation of his subjects went to oppose him, as Josephus reports. “Kingdom” is kept so that the link with “the kingdom of God” in verse 11 stays audible.

text.q: He called ten of his slaves, gave them ten minas, and said to them, ‘Do business with this until I come back.’

verse.note: The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired employee, and standard lexicons gloss it as “slave.” Most English versions soften it to “servant.” In the ancient world slaves were often entrusted with managing money and business, as here.

A mina was a sum of one hundred drachmas, roughly three to four months’ wages for a day laborer. Each slave receives one mina. It is a far smaller sum than the talent in the similar parable in Matthew 25, which is why the king calls it “a very small matter.”

text.q: But his fellow citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him to say, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us.’
When he returned, having received the kingdom, he ordered the slaves to whom he had given the money to be called to him, so that he might learn what they had gained by doing business.
The first came forward and said, ‘Master, your mina has earned ten minas more.’
He said to him, ‘Well done, good slave! Because you have been faithful in a very small matter, you are to have authority over ten cities.’
The second came and said, ‘Your mina, master, has made five minas.’
He said to this one too, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’
Then the other came and said, ‘Master, here is your mina, which I kept laid away in a cloth,
for I was afraid of you, because you are a harsh man: you take up what you did not lay down and reap what you did not sow.’
He said to him, ‘Out of your own mouth I judge you, wicked slave! You knew, did you, that I am a harsh man, taking up what I did not lay down and reaping what I did not sow?
Then why did you not put my money in the bank? Then when I came I would have collected it with interest.’
And to those standing by he said, ‘Take the mina from him and give it to the one who has the ten minas.’
They said to him, ‘Master, he has ten minas!’
‘I tell you that to everyone who has, more will be given, but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.

verse.note: The Greek does not mark who speaks this sentence. It is rendered here as the king’s reply to the bystanders’ objection, since verse 27 continues in the king’s voice. It can also be read as Jesus stepping outside the story to state its point to his own hearers; the same saying appears on Jesus’ lips in Luke 8:18.

text.q: But as for these enemies of mine who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them in front of me.’”

verse.text: After saying this, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem.
When he came near Bethphage and Bethany, at the hill called the Mount of Olives, he sent two of the disciples,
saying, “Go into the village opposite, and as you enter it you will find a colt tied there, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it.

text.q: And if anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ you shall say this: ‘The Lord needs it.’”

note.traditional: The Lord has need of it

verse.note: The Greek can also be construed as “Its master needs it,” with “its” attached to “Lord” rather than to “needs.” The same word, in the plural, is used for the colt’s “owners” in verse 33, so the reply sets one claim of ownership against another. Most translations render as here.

verse.text: Those who were sent went off and found it just as he had told them.
As they were untying the colt, its owners said to them, “Why are you untying the colt?”
They said, “The Lord needs it.”
They brought it to Jesus, and throwing their cloaks on the colt, they set Jesus on it.
As he went along, they kept spreading their cloaks on the road.
As he was now drawing near, at the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began joyfully to praise God with a loud voice for all the deeds of power they had seen,
verse.note: The Greek is the ordinary word for “power,” used here of concrete acts that display it. “Deeds of power” keeps that connection visible; “miracles” and “mighty works” are equally acceptable renderings, and there is no dispute about the meaning.

verse.text: saying, “Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!”

note.term: Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord

verse.note: The disciples adapt Psalm 118:26, a psalm sung by pilgrims at the festivals: “Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.” Luke’s wording adds “the king,” making the royal claim explicit. The second line recalls the angels’ song at Jesus’ birth in Luke 2:14.

verse.text: Some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.”
He answered, “I tell you, if these are silent, the stones will cry out.”
As he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it,
saying, “If only you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace—but now they have been hidden from your eyes.

text.q: For days will come upon you when your enemies will throw up a palisade against you and surround you and hem you in on every side,
and they will dash you to the ground, you and your children within you, and will not leave one stone upon another within you, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation.”

verse.note: In the Greek Scriptures a “visitation” is God’s coming to look upon his people, whether to rescue or to judge. Here it is the gracious kind: God has come to Jerusalem in Jesus, and the city has not recognized it. Luke uses the related verb in the same sense in 1:68 and 7:16, “God has visited his people.”

verse.text: Then he entered the temple and began to drive out those who were selling,
saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be a house of prayer,’ but you have made it ‘a den of bandits.’”
verse.note: The Greek word denotes a violent, often armed plunderer such as a highwayman, and is distinct from the word for a thief who steals by stealth. Most modern versions use “robbers,” which is not wrong; “bandits” keeps the note of violence and outlawry. Jesus joins Isaiah 56:7 to Jeremiah 7:11, where the “den” is the hideout in which bandits feel safe after their crimes.

verse.text: He was teaching daily in the temple. The chief priests and the scribes were seeking to destroy him, as were the leading men of the people,
but they could not find anything they could do, for all the people hung on his words as they listened.
One day, as he was teaching the people in the temple and announcing the good news, the chief priests and the scribes came up with the elders
verse.note: The Greek verb was an ordinary word for bringing or publicly announcing good news. “Gospel” has since become a religious term and the name of a kind of book, so “good news” is closer to what a first-century hearer understood. Many modern translations make the same choice.

verse.text: and said to him, “Tell us by what authority you are doing these things, or who it is that gave you this authority.”
He answered them, “I will also ask you a question, and you tell me:

text.q: The baptism of John—was it from heaven or from human beings?”

verse.text: They discussed it among themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why did you not believe him?’

text.q: But if we say, ‘From human beings,’ all the people will stone us, for they are convinced that John was a prophet.”

verse.text: So they answered that they did not know where it was from.
And Jesus said to them, “Neither am I telling you by what authority I am doing these things.”
Then he began to tell the people this parable: “A man planted a vineyard, leased it to tenants, and went abroad for a long time.

text.q: When the season came, he sent a slave to the tenants so that they would give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed.

verse.note: The Greek word names a person owned by a master, not a hired employee. Most older English versions say “servant”; several modern ones use “slave” here. The owner’s right to send these men and the tenants’ contempt for them both fit that status.

text.q: He went on to send another slave; but that one too they beat and treated shamefully and sent away empty-handed.
He went on to send a third; this one too they wounded and threw out.
Then the owner of the vineyard said, ‘What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will respect him.’
But when the tenants saw him, they reasoned with one another, saying, ‘This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance will be ours.’
So they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What then will the owner of the vineyard do to them?

verse.text: He will come and destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” When they heard this, they said, “May it never happen!”
But he looked straight at them and said, “What then is this that is written: ‘The stone that the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone’?
verse.note: The quotation is from Psalm 118:22. The Greek is literally “head of the corner,” which may mean a foundation stone at the corner of a building or the stone that crowns it, such as a capstone or keystone. Scholars are divided; either way it is the most important stone in the structure.

text.q: Everyone who falls on that stone will be shattered, and it will crush anyone on whom it falls.”

verse.note: The verb ordinarily means “winnow,” and from that “scatter like chaff.” Most lexicons and translations take it here as “crush,” in line with the image of a falling stone and with a Greek version of Daniel 2:44, where the same verb is used of a kingdom that shatters all others. “Scatter him like chaff” is a possible alternative.

verse.text: The scribes and the chief priests sought to lay hands on him at that very hour, but they feared the people; for they realized that he had told this parable against them.
So they watched him closely and sent spies who pretended to be righteous, so that they might catch him in something he said and so hand him over to the jurisdiction and authority of the governor.
verse.note: This is the ordinary Greek verb for transferring someone into another’s custody or power. The Gospels use the same word for what Judas, the priests and Pilate each do to Jesus, and this translation renders it “hand over” throughout so that the chain is visible.

verse.text: They questioned him, saying, “Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly and show no partiality, but teach the way of God in truth.

text.q: Are we permitted to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?”

note.term: Are we permitted to pay tribute
note.traditional: Is it lawful for us to give tribute

verse.note: The question is whether God’s law allows it, not whether Roman law does; “lawful” can suggest the latter to a modern reader. The word for “tribute” denotes the tax a subject people paid to its foreign ruler, which was a standing grievance in Judea. A yes would discredit Jesus with the people, and a no would be grounds for a charge before the governor.

verse.text: But he saw through their craftiness and said to them,
“Show me a denarius. Whose image and inscription does it have?” They answered, “Caesar’s.”
verse.note: A Roman silver coin, roughly a day’s wage for a laborer. Those of the reigning emperor Tiberius carried his portrait and an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus. Jesus’ questioners can produce one even though they are in the temple.

verse.text: He said to them, “Then give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”
verse.note: The questioners asked about “giving” tribute, but Jesus answers with a stronger verb that means to pay what is owed or return what belongs to someone. “Give back” keeps that shift; many modern versions have simply “give.”

verse.text: And they were not able to catch him in what he said in front of the people; and marveling at his answer, they fell silent.
Some of the Sadducees, who deny that there is a resurrection, came up and questioned him,
saying, “Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies leaving a wife but no children, the man should take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother.

note.term: raise up offspring for his brother
note.traditional: raise up seed unto his brother

verse.note: The reference is to the law of levirate marriage in Deuteronomy 25:5–6. When a married man died without a son, his brother was to marry the widow, and the first son born counted as the dead man’s heir. The Sadducees, who accepted no resurrection, use this law to build a case meant to make the idea look absurd.

text.q: Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife and died childless;
then the second
and the third took her; and in the same way all seven left no children and died.
Finally the woman died too.
So in the resurrection, whose wife does the woman become? For all seven had her as wife.”

verse.text: Jesus said to them, “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage,
verse.note: The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era, not the physical world. Jesus is using the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come. “Children of” (literally “sons of”) is a Semitic idiom for those who belong to something, and it recurs in verse 36. Most modern translations also have “age” here.

text.q: but those who are counted worthy to attain that age and the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage.
For they cannot die anymore, because they are equal to angels, and they are children of God, being children of the resurrection.
But that the dead are raised, even Moses made known in the passage about the bush, where he calls the Lord ‘the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob.’

note.term: in the passage about the bush

verse.note: The Greek says only “at the bush.” Before chapter and verse numbers existed, a passage of Scripture was cited by a key word; this one is the burning bush account in Exodus 3. Jesus argues from the books of Moses because the Sadducees gave them the highest authority.

text.q: He is not God of the dead but of the living, for to him all are alive.”

verse.text: Then some of the scribes answered, “Teacher, you have spoken well.”
For they no longer dared to ask him anything.
Then he said to them, “How can they say that the Messiah is David’s son?
verse.note: The Greek word here is a title, “the anointed one,” for the king Israel expected, and the question is about that figure’s descent. “Messiah” conveys the title; “Christ” now sounds like a name. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

text.q: For David himself says in the book of Psalms, ‘The Lord said to my Lord: “Sit at my right hand

note.term: The Lord said to my Lord
note.traditional: The LORD said unto my Lord

verse.note: The quotation is Psalm 110:1. In Greek the same word, “lord,” appears twice; in the Hebrew the first is the divine name and the second is the ordinary word for a master or superior. Jesus’ argument turns on the second: David, the supposed author, calls the coming king his own lord.

text.q: until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.”’
David, then, calls him ‘Lord’; so how is he his son?”

verse.text: While all the people were listening, he said to the disciples,

text.q: “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and love greetings in the marketplaces and the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets,
who devour widows’ houses and for show pray at length. These will receive a harsher judgment.”

verse.text: Looking up, he saw rich people putting their gifts into the treasury.
He also saw a needy widow putting in two small copper coins there,
verse.note: The Greek names the coin: the lepton, the smallest coin in circulation in Judea. Two of them together came to roughly one sixty-fourth of a laborer’s daily wage. The point is that the gift was almost worthless in money terms and yet was everything the widow had.

verse.text: and he said, “I tell you truly, this poor widow has put in more than all of them.

text.q: For all of these added to the gifts out of their surplus, but she, out of her need, put in all she had to live on.”

verse.text: And when some were speaking about the temple, how it was adorned with beautiful stones and votive offerings, he said,

text.q: “These things that you are looking at—days will come when not one stone will be left on another that will not be thrown down.”

verse.text: They asked him, “Teacher, when then will these things be, and what will be the sign when they are about to happen?”
He said, “Watch out that you are not led astray. For many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he,’ and, ‘The time has come near.’ Do not go after them.

text.q: When you hear of wars and uprisings, do not be terrified; for these things must happen first, but the end will not come at once.”

verse.text: Then he said to them, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom.
verse.note: One Greek word lies behind both “nation” and “Gentiles” in this chapter. It means a people or nation, and in the plural it often means the non-Jewish peoples. It is rendered “nation” here and in verse 25, and in verse 24 both “nations” (where the captives are scattered) and “Gentiles” (who trample Jerusalem); a Greek reader heard the same word each time.

text.q: There will be great earthquakes, and in various places famines and plagues; there will be terrors and great signs from heaven.
But before all this they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, handing you over to the synagogues and prisons, and you will be led away before kings and governors because of my name.

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for transferring someone into another’s custody or power. Many versions render it “betrayed” in verse 16, where family members are the agents; that names the treachery the context implies, but it hides the fact that the same word is used in verse 12 and, throughout the Gospels, of what is done to Jesus himself. “Hand over” is the basic sense given in the standard lexicons.

text.q: This will turn out for you as an opportunity to testify.
So resolve in your hearts not to prepare your defense in advance,
for I myself will give you a mouth and a wisdom that none of your opponents will be able to resist or contradict.
You will be handed over even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and they will put some of you to death,
and you will be hated by everyone because of my name.
Yet not a hair of your head will perish.
By your endurance gain your lives.

verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between a command (“gain”) and a future (“you will gain”); the two forms differ by a single letter. The Greek text translated here reads the command, while many modern versions follow the future. The sense is much the same either way: endurance is the means by which life is secured.

The Greek word most often means a person’s life or living self rather than an immaterial part of the person, and that is the sense wherever it is saved, lost or gained. Older versions and some modern ones have “souls” here; others, as here, have “lives”. After the warning that some will be put to death, the life gained is evidently more than physical survival.

text.q: But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near.

verse.note: Roman armies besieged Jerusalem and destroyed the city and its temple in AD 70. Where Mark and Matthew speak at this point of “the abomination of desolation”, Luke speaks plainly of armies and of the city’s desolation. Scholars disagree about whether this wording reflects knowledge of the event or simply draws on Old Testament descriptions of sieges.

text.q: Then those in Judea must flee to the mountains, those inside the city must leave it, and those in the countryside must not enter it,
for these are days of vengeance, so that all that is written may be fulfilled.
Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing in those days! For there will be great distress on the land and wrath against this people,

note.traditional: in the land / on the earth

verse.note: The Greek word means both “land” and “earth”. Because the verse goes on to speak of “this people” and the surrounding verses concern Judea and Jerusalem, it is rendered “land” here; some versions have “earth”. In verses 25 and 35, where the scope is worldwide, the same word is rendered “earth”.

text.q: and they will fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all the nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled by Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.
And there will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth anguish among nations bewildered by the roar of the sea and the surging waves,
people fainting from fear and foreboding of what is coming upon the world, for the powers of the heavens will be shaken.
And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory.

note.term: the Son of Man coming in a cloud

verse.note: The language echoes Daniel 7:13, where “one like a son of man” comes with the clouds of heaven and is given everlasting dominion. In the Scriptures a cloud regularly accompanies the presence of God. A first-century Jewish hearer would have recognized the allusion.

text.q: When these things begin to happen, stand up straight and lift your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”

verse.text: And he told them a parable: “Look at the fig tree and all the trees.

text.q: As soon as they put out leaves, you see it and know for yourselves that summer is already near.
So also you, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.
Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until everything has happened.

verse.note: The natural sense of the Greek is the people alive at the time of speaking, and most scholars take it so, differing over what “everything” then covers (the fall of Jerusalem, or also the coming of the Son of Man). Others have proposed “this race” (the Jewish people), “this kind of people”, or the generation that sees the final signs. The traditional rendering is kept because it is what the word ordinarily meant.

text.q: Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.
But watch yourselves, so that your hearts are not weighed down with carousing and drunkenness and the worries of daily life, and that day does not come upon you suddenly
like a trap. For it will come upon all who live on the face of the whole earth.

note.term: like a trap. For it will come
note.traditional: For as a snare shall it come

verse.note: Manuscripts differ over the position of the word “for”, and so over where the sentence divides. In the text translated here “like a trap” completes verse 34 (“that day does not come upon you suddenly like a trap”). In the other reading it begins a new sentence: “For like a trap it will come upon all …”. The image probably echoes Isaiah 24:17.

text.q: But stay awake at all times, praying that you may have the strength to escape all these things that are about to happen, and to stand before the Son of Man.”

verse.text: By day he was teaching in the temple, and at night he would go out and stay on the hill called the Mount of Olives.
And all the people would come to him early in the morning in the temple to hear him.
Now the Festival of Unleavened Bread, which is called Passover, was drawing near.
And the chief priests and the scribes were looking for a way to do away with him, for they were afraid of the people.
Then Satan entered Judas, the one called Iscariot, who belonged to the number of the Twelve.
He went away and discussed with the chief priests and the captains of the guard how he might hand him over to them.
verse.note: Most English versions say “betray” when Judas is the subject. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for handing someone into another’s custody, and the Gospels use the same word for what the priests and Pilate later do with Jesus; “hand over” lets the reader see that chain. Some scholars defend “betray” as a legitimate contextual sense, and the treachery is clear from the story either way.

verse.text: They were delighted and agreed to give him money.
He consented, and began looking for an opportunity to hand him over to them away from the crowd.
Then the day of Unleavened Bread came, on which the Passover lamb had to be sacrificed.
And he sent Peter and John, saying, “Go and prepare the Passover for us, so that we may eat it.”
They said to him, “Where do you want us to prepare it?”
He said to them, “Look, when you have entered the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house that he enters,

text.q: and say to the owner of the house, ‘The Teacher says to you, “Where is the guest room where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?”’
And he will show you a large upstairs room, furnished. Prepare it there.”

verse.text: They went and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
When the hour came, he reclined at the table, and the apostles with him.
And he said to them, “I have longed with all my heart to eat this Passover with you before I suffer;

text.q: for I tell you that I will certainly not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.”

verse.text: Then, receiving a cup, he gave thanks and said, “Take this and share it among yourselves;

text.q: for I tell you, from now on I will certainly not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.”

verse.text: And he took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body, [which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
verse.note: The brackets enclose the words from “which is given for you” to the end of verse 20. One early Greek manuscript and several Old Latin witnesses lack these words, so that Jesus’ saying over the bread ends at “This is my body.” The great majority of manuscripts, including the earliest, contain them, and most scholars today consider them original, though the question is still debated.

verse.text: And he did the same with the cup after the supper, saying, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood.]

text.q: But look, the hand of the one who is handing me over is with me on the table.
For the Son of Man is going as it has been determined, but woe to that man through whom he is handed over!”

verse.text: And they began to discuss among themselves which of them it could be who was going to do this.
A dispute also arose among them over which of them was considered the greatest.
But he said to them, “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called Benefactors.
verse.note: One Greek word means both “nations” and, in the plural from a Jewish standpoint, “Gentiles,” the non-Jewish peoples. Either fits here, and “the kings of the nations” is equally possible; the traditional rendering is kept.

“Benefactor” was a formal title of honor in the Greek-speaking world, given to kings and wealthy patrons and borne by several Hellenistic rulers. The remark is ironic: those who dominate their subjects are publicly honored as their benefactors. The verb can also be read as “call themselves.”

text.q: But not so with you. Rather, let the greatest among you become like the youngest, and the one who leads like the one who serves.
For who is greater, the one who reclines at the table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines? Yet I am among you as the one who serves.
You are the ones who have stayed with me through my times of testing.

verse.note: In the usage of the period this word mainly means a putting to the proof, an ordeal that shows whether someone will stay faithful. English “temptation” has narrowed to enticement to sin, so the word is rendered “testing” here and in verses 40 and 46, where most versions have “temptation” and some have “time of trial.” Lexicons recognize both senses, and the two overlap in the Gethsemane sayings.

text.q: And I confer on you a kingdom, just as my Father conferred one on me,

verse.note: “A kingdom” may be the object of both verbs, as rendered here, or only of the second: “I confer on you, just as my Father conferred a kingdom on me, that you may eat and drink at my table.” The verb is related to the word for “covenant” in verse 20 and was used of making a covenant or a will.

text.q: so that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and you will sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
Simon, Simon, look—Satan has demanded to have all of you, to sift you like wheat;

verse.note: The Greek “you” is plural in this verse—Satan has asked for all the disciples—but singular throughout verse 32, where Jesus speaks of his prayer for Simon in particular. English “you” hides the shift, so “all of” is supplied here.

text.q: but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And you, once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.”

verse.text: But he said to him, “Lord, with you I am ready to go both to prison and to death.”
He said, “I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know me.”
And he said to them, “When I sent you out without purse or bag or sandals, did you lack anything?” They said, “Nothing.”
He said to them, “But now, the one who has a purse must take it, and likewise a bag; and the one who has none must sell his cloak and buy a sword.

text.q: For I tell you that this which is written must be brought to completion in me: ‘And he was counted among the lawless.’ For indeed what concerns me is reaching its completion.”

note.traditional: has its fulfillment; have an end

verse.note: The quotation is from Isaiah 53:12. The closing clause is literally “what concerns me has an end.” It can mean that what is written about Jesus is being fulfilled, as rendered here, or that his life and work are coming to their end; the Greek noun echoes the verb “brought to completion” earlier in the verse.

verse.text: They said, “Lord, look, here are two swords.” He said to them, “It is enough.”
verse.note: The reply can be taken at face value—two swords are sufficient—or as a curt end to the conversation, “Enough of this!”, because the disciples have taken the saying about swords too literally. Many interpreters prefer the second in light of verse 51; the rendering leaves both open.

verse.text: Then he went out and made his way, as was his custom, to the Mount of Olives, and the disciples followed him.
When he reached the place, he said to them, “Pray that you may not enter into testing.”
And he withdrew from them about a stone’s throw, knelt down, and began to pray,
saying, “Father, if you are willing, take this cup away from me. Yet not my will but yours be done.”
And an angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him.

note.term: an angel from heaven appeared to him

verse.note: Verses 43–44 are absent from several of the earliest and most valued manuscripts, are marked as doubtful in some others, and appear after Matthew 26:39 in one group of manuscripts. They were, however, known to Christian writers as early as the second century. Scholars are divided over whether Luke wrote them or they are a very early addition; the edition translated here prints them without brackets.

verse.text: And being in anguish, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground.
When he rose from prayer and came to the disciples, he found them asleep from grief,
and he said to them, “Why are you sleeping? Get up and pray, so that you may not enter into testing.”
While he was still speaking, suddenly there was a crowd, and the one called Judas, one of the Twelve, was leading them. He came up to Jesus to kiss him,
but Jesus said to him, “Judas, is it with a kiss that you hand over the Son of Man?”
When those around him saw what was about to happen, they said, “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?”
And one of them struck the slave of the high priest and cut off his right ear.
But Jesus answered, “Stop! No more of this.” And he touched the ear and healed him.

note.traditional: Suffer ye thus far; No more of this

verse.note: The Greek is terse, literally “Allow as far as this.” It is usually understood as a command to the disciples to stop the violence, as rendered here. It could instead mean “Let them go this far,” that is, allow the arrest to proceed.

verse.text: Then Jesus said to the chief priests, captains of the temple guard, and elders who had come out against him, “Have you come out with swords and clubs as if against a bandit?
verse.note: The Greek word denotes an armed, violent plunderer such as a highwayman or brigand, as distinct from a thief who steals by stealth. Most modern versions say “robber,” which is not wrong but can suggest a burglar. The word was also applied to insurgents, and some translations render it “rebel” here; that overtone is possible but not certain.

text.q: Day after day, when I was with you in the temple, you did not lay a hand on me. But this is your hour, and the authority of darkness.”

verse.text: Having seized him, they led him away and brought him into the high priest’s house. Peter was following at a distance.
When they had lit a fire in the middle of the courtyard and sat down together, Peter sat down among them.
A slave girl saw him sitting in the firelight, looked closely at him, and said, “This man was with him too.”
But he denied it, saying, “I do not know him, woman.”
A little later someone else saw him and said, “You are one of them too.” But Peter said, “Man, I am not!”
About an hour later another man began to insist, “Certainly this man was with him too, for he is a Galilean.”
But Peter said, “Man, I do not know what you are talking about.” And immediately, while he was still speaking, a rooster crowed.
And the Lord turned and looked straight at Peter, and Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said to him, “Before a rooster crows today, you will deny me three times.”
And he went outside and wept bitterly.
Now the men who were holding him began mocking him and beating him.
They blindfolded him and kept asking, “Prophesy! Who is it that hit you?”
And they said many other insulting things against him.
verse.note: In first-century Greek this verb meant abusive or demeaning speech against anyone, not only against God. Here the guards are jeering at a prisoner to his face, so “insulting” gives the sense. Versions that keep “blaspheming” reflect the Christian reader’s awareness of who is being abused, which Luke may also intend.

verse.text: When day came, the assembly of the elders of the people gathered, both chief priests and scribes, and they led him away to their council,
saying, “If you are the Messiah, tell us.” But he said to them, “If I tell you, you will certainly not believe;
verse.note: The Greek word is the one traditionally rendered “Christ.” Here it is a title under examination—the anointed king Israel expected—not a name, and “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

text.q: and if I ask a question, you will certainly not answer.
But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.”

verse.text: They all said, “Are you, then, the Son of God?” He said to them, “You say that I am.”

note.traditional: Ye say that I am; You say that I am

verse.note: The reply neither plainly affirms nor denies; it throws the statement back on the questioners, and the council treats it as an admission in verse 71. The Greek could also be read “You yourselves say it, because I am.”

verse.text: They said, “What further need do we have of testimony? For we ourselves have heard it from his own mouth.”
Then the whole assembly of them rose and led him to Pilate.
They began to accuse him, saying, “We found this man subverting our nation, forbidding the payment of taxes to Caesar, and saying that he himself is the Messiah, a king.”
verse.note: The Greek word is the one traditionally rendered “Christ”. Here it is a title, the anointed king Israel expected, and that title is the substance of the charge, so “Messiah” is used, as in several modern translations. The Greek has no article, and the phrase could also be read “an anointed king”.

The Greek word rendered “nation” here, of the Jewish people as a political unit, is the same word that in the plural is usually translated “Gentiles”. English needs two words for what Greek expresses with one.

verse.text: Pilate asked him, “Are you the king of the Jews?” He answered him, “You say so.”
Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds, “I find no ground for a charge against this man.”
But they kept insisting, “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, starting from Galilee and reaching as far as here.”
When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean,
and on learning that he was under Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself also in Jerusalem in those days.
verse.note: This is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea under Rome. He was presumably in Jerusalem for Passover. Because Jesus was a Galilean, Pilate could refer the case to him. Only Luke records this hearing.

verse.text: When Herod saw Jesus he was very glad, for he had been wanting to see him for a long time because of what he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him.
He questioned him at length, but Jesus gave him no answer.
The chief priests and the scribes stood there, accusing him vehemently.
Herod too, with his troops, treated him with contempt and mocked him; then he dressed him in a splendid robe and sent him back to Pilate.
That same day Herod and Pilate became friends with each other, for before this they had been enemies.
Pilate called together the chief priests, the rulers, and the people,

and said to them, “You brought this man to me as someone who was leading the people astray. And look, I examined him in your presence and found in this man no ground for the charges you bring against him.

text.q: Nor did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, he has done nothing that deserves death.
So I will have him disciplined and then release him.”

verse.note: The verb ordinarily means to bring up, instruct or correct a child. Here it is Pilate’s mild term for a beating given as a warning before release, lighter than the scourging that preceded crucifixion. Many versions spell out the sense as “flog” or generalize it to “punish”; “disciplined” keeps the understatement of the Greek.

verse.text: But they all cried out together, “Away with this man! Release Barabbas to us!”

note.term: But they all cried out together

verse.note: Verse 17 (“Now he was obliged to release one prisoner to them at the festival”) is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not in the Greek text translated here. It is generally regarded as a later explanatory addition based on Matthew 27:15 and Mark 15:6.

verse.text: This was a man who had been thrown into prison because of an uprising that had taken place in the city, and for murder.
Pilate addressed them again, wanting to release Jesus,
but they kept shouting, “Crucify, crucify him!”
A third time he said to them, “Why, what evil has this man done? I have found in him no ground for a death sentence. So I will have him disciplined and then release him.”
But they pressed him with loud voices, demanding that he be crucified, and their voices prevailed.
So Pilate ruled that their demand should be granted.
He released the man who had been thrown into prison for uprising and murder, the one they were demanding, and he handed Jesus over to their will.
As they led him away, they seized a certain Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid the cross on him to carry behind Jesus.
A great crowd of the people followed him, among them women who were mourning and lamenting him.
But Jesus turned to them and said, “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me; weep instead for yourselves and for your children,

text.q: for look, days are coming when they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren, the wombs that never bore and the breasts that never nursed!’
Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us!’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us!’
For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?”

verse.text: Two others, criminals, were also led away to be put to death with him.
When they came to the place called the Skull, they crucified him there with the criminals, one on his right and one on his left.
Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” And they cast lots to divide his clothes among themselves.

note.term: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

verse.note: This prayer is absent from several early and important manuscripts, including Papyrus 75 and Codex Vaticanus, and present in others. Scholars are divided on whether Luke wrote it or whether it is a very early tradition added to his Gospel.

verse.text: The people stood watching. The rulers too were sneering at him, saying, “He saved others; let him save himself, if this is the Messiah of God, the Chosen One!”
The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine
and saying, “If you are the king of the Jews, save yourself!”
There was also an inscription over him: “This is the king of the Jews.”
One of the criminals who were hanging there kept insulting him: “Are you not the Messiah? Save yourself and us!”
verse.note: The Greek verb covers abusive speech against anyone, human or divine, whereas modern English “blaspheme” is confined to irreverence toward God. Here the criminal is taunting Jesus to his face, so “insulting” is used. Modern versions vary among “railed at”, “derided” and “hurled insults at”.

verse.text: But the other answered, rebuking him, “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same sentence?

text.q: And we are here justly, for we are getting what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong.”

verse.text: Then he said, “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom.”

note.term: when you come into your kingdom

verse.note: The Greek text translated here reads literally “in your kingdom”, which can mean either “when you enter your kingdom” or “when you come with your kingly power”, that is, at a future return as king. Some early manuscripts read “into your kingdom”, which favors the first sense. The English phrase chosen can carry either.

verse.text: He said to him, “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise.”
verse.note: Greek manuscripts had no punctuation, so “today” could in principle go with “I tell you” (“Truly I tell you today, you will be with me”). Almost all translators and commentators take it with what follows, since the “Truly I tell you” formula never elsewhere carries a time word and the promise answers the man’s indefinite “when”.

The word, borrowed from Persian, meant an enclosed park or garden, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for the garden of Eden. In Jewish usage of the period it had come to name the place of blessedness where the righteous dead are with God.

verse.text: It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour,
verse.note: Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about noon and the ninth hour about three in the afternoon. The word rendered “land” can also mean “earth”; the scope of the darkness is not specified.

verse.text: for the sun’s light failed. And the curtain of the sanctuary was torn down the middle.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts say the sun “failed” or “gave out”; many later ones read “the sun was darkened”. The verb was also the usual term for an eclipse, but it need not be technical here, and a solar eclipse cannot occur at the full moon of Passover.

Greek has one word for the whole temple complex with its courts and another, used here, for the building at its center where God was understood to dwell. Most English versions render both “temple”; “sanctuary” keeps the distinction. The curtain is most often taken to be the one that screened off the innermost room, though some think the curtain at the entrance of the building is meant.

verse.text: Then Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Father, into your hands I entrust my spirit.” Having said this, he breathed his last.
When the centurion saw what had happened, he glorified God, saying, “Truly this man was righteous.”
verse.note: The Greek adjective means both “righteous” and, in a legal setting, “innocent”, and many versions choose “innocent” here after Pilate’s three declarations that Jesus had done nothing deserving death. “Righteous” is kept because it includes innocence and matches the description of Joseph in verse 50. Greek uses one word-family where English has two; “justly” in verse 41 is the related adverb.

verse.text: And all the crowds that had gathered for this spectacle, when they saw what had happened, went home beating their breasts.
But all who knew him stood at a distance, along with the women who had followed him from Galilee, watching these things.
Now there was a man named Joseph, a member of the council, a good and righteous man—
he had not agreed with their decision and their action—from Arimathea, a town of the Jews, who was waiting for the kingdom of God.
This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
Then he took it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and laid him in a tomb cut in the rock, where no one had yet been laid.
It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was about to begin.

note.term: the Sabbath was about to begin

verse.note: “Preparation” was the name for the day before the Sabbath, that is, Friday. The Sabbath began at sunset. The Greek verb literally means “was dawning” and is used here loosely for the start of the day, so the burial was carried out in the last hours of Friday afternoon.

verse.text: The women who had come with him from Galilee followed behind and saw the tomb and how his body was laid.
Then they went back and prepared spices and perfumed oils. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.
But on the first day of the week, at early dawn, the women came to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared.
They found the stone rolled away from the tomb,
but when they went in they did not find the body.
While they were at a loss about this, suddenly two men in dazzling clothing stood beside them.
verse.note: Luke calls the figures “men,” but their dazzling clothing marks them as heavenly messengers, and verse 23 refers to them as angels. Their words are treated here as angelic speech.

verse.text: They were terrified and bowed their faces to the ground, but the men said to them, “Why do you look for the living among the dead?

text.q: He is not here, but has been raised. Remember how he told you while he was still in Galilee,
that the Son of Man must be handed over into the hands of sinful people and be crucified and on the third day rise.”

verse.text: And they remembered his words,
and returning from the tomb they reported all these things to the eleven and to all the rest.
They were Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the other women with them. They kept telling the apostles these things.
But these words seemed to them like nonsense, and they did not believe the women.
But Peter got up and ran to the tomb. Stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths by themselves, and he went home, wondering at what had happened.

note.term: But Peter got up and ran to the tomb

verse.note: This verse is missing from a small group of witnesses, mainly Codex Bezae and some Old Latin copies, and older critical editions doubted it. It is present in the earliest surviving copies and the great majority of manuscripts, and most scholars now accept it as original. Several short phrases elsewhere in this chapter have a similar pattern of evidence.

verse.text: Now that same day two of them were on their way to a village called Emmaus, sixty stadia from Jerusalem,
verse.note: A stadion was roughly 185 meters, so sixty stadia is about seven miles or eleven kilometers. Some manuscripts read “one hundred and sixty,” and the site of Emmaus is uncertain.

verse.text: and they were talking with each other about all these things that had taken place.
While they were talking and discussing, Jesus himself came near and walked along with them,
but their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
He said to them, “What are these words you are exchanging with each other as you walk?” They stood still, looking gloomy.
Then one of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only visitor to Jerusalem who has not learned what has happened there in these days?”
verse.note: The verb means to live somewhere as a foreigner or temporary resident, and Cleopas probably takes the stranger for a Passover pilgrim. The Greek can also be read “Are you the only one living in Jerusalem who does not know,” or “Are you only a visitor to Jerusalem, that you do not know.”

verse.text: He said to them, “What things?” They said to him, “The things about Jesus the Nazarene, who was a prophet powerful in deed and word before God and all the people,

text.q: and how our chief priests and rulers handed him over to be sentenced to death, and crucified him.
But we were hoping that he was the one who was going to set Israel free. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.

verse.note: The traditional “redeem” is now heard mainly as a term for salvation from sin. In the Greek Old Testament the verb is used of God freeing Israel from slavery in Egypt and from its enemies, and the two disciples are voicing a hope for the nation’s deliverance. Most translations keep “redeem”; the meaning itself is not disputed.

text.q: What is more, some women of our group astounded us. They were at the tomb early in the morning,
and when they did not find his body, they came back saying that they had even seen a vision of angels, who say that he is alive.
Some of those with us went off to the tomb and found it just as the women had said, but him they did not see.”

verse.text: And he said to them, “How foolish you are, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken!

text.q: Was it not necessary for the Messiah to suffer these things and enter into his glory?”

verse.note: The Greek word is the one traditionally rendered “Christ.” Here it is a title for the anointed king Israel expected, and the question is what that figure had to undergo, so “Messiah” conveys what a first-century hearer understood. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep “Christ” where it functions as a name.

verse.text: Then, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he explained to them the things about himself in all the Scriptures.
They came near the village where they were going, and he acted as though he were going farther.
But they urged him strongly, saying, “Stay with us, because it is nearly evening and the day is already far gone.” So he went in to stay with them.
When he had reclined at the table with them, he took the bread and said the blessing, and he broke it and began giving it to them.
verse.note: The Greek has no object. At a Jewish meal the blessing over bread is addressed to God, who is praised for providing it; it is not pronounced on the bread. The same verb is rendered “blessed” in verse 50 and “blessing” in verse 53.

verse.text: Then their eyes were opened and they recognized him, and he vanished from their sight.
They said to each other, “Were not our hearts burning within us as he was talking to us on the road, as he was opening the Scriptures to us?”
They got up that very hour and returned to Jerusalem, and they found the eleven and those with them gathered together,
who were saying, “The Lord really has been raised, and has appeared to Simon!”
Then they themselves related what had happened on the road and how he was made known to them in the breaking of the bread.
While they were saying these things, he himself stood among them.
verse.note: Most manuscripts, and most translations, continue “and said to them, ‘Peace be with you.’” The Greek edition translated here omits the words, following a small group of witnesses, on the view that they were added from John 20:19. Many scholars regard them as original to Luke.

verse.text: Startled and terrified, they thought they were seeing a ghost.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary word for “spirit,” which older translations keep here. In this context it means the disembodied spirit of a dead person, for which the natural English word is “ghost.” Many modern translations do the same.

verse.text: He said to them, “Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts?

text.q: Look at my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me and see, because a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.”

verse.text: [And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.]

note.term: [And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.]

verse.note: The brackets mark words that the Greek edition translated here regards as doubtful. The verse is missing from a few witnesses, chiefly Codex Bezae and some Old Latin copies, and closely resembles John 20:20. It is found in the earliest and most numerous manuscripts, and many scholars accept it as original.

verse.text: While they still could not believe it for joy and were amazed, he said to them, “Do you have anything here to eat?”
They gave him a piece of broiled fish,
and he took it and ate it in front of them.
Then he said to them, “These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you: that everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.”
Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures,
and he said to them, “This is what is written: the Messiah is to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day,

text.q: and turning back and forgiveness of sins are to be proclaimed in his name to all the nations—beginning from Jerusalem.

verse.note: “Repentance” now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets’ call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep “repentance” as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.

The same Greek word means both “nations” and “Gentiles,” the non-Jewish peoples. “All the nations” is used here because the scope is the whole world, starting from Jerusalem; “all the Gentiles” is also a possible reading.

text.q: You are witnesses of these things.
And look, I am sending the promise of my Father upon you. But you, stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.”

verse.text: Then he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them.
While he was blessing them, he parted from them [and was carried up into heaven].
verse.note: The bracketed words here and in verse 52 are absent from a few early witnesses and are marked as doubtful in the Greek edition translated here. Most manuscripts, including the earliest, contain them, and most recent scholars accept them as original.

verse.text: And they [worshiped him and] returned to Jerusalem with great joy,
and they were continually in the temple, blessing God.
